            RUPERTA ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
            1. Corticospinal Tract

            A. Place an “x” over the hand/arm region of the precentral gyrus on your drawn diagram.

                  The "x" should be placed on the lateral aspect of the precentral gyrus, corresponding to the somatotopic representation of the hand and arm.
                    Why: The precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex) is organized somatotopically, meaning different areas control different parts of the body. The lateral aspect of the precentral gyrus specifically represents the hand and arm. Therefore, a lesion in this region would primarily affect motor control of the hand and arm.

            B. Describe the deficit you would expect to see in your patient with the above lesion (note specifics such as body (arm, trunk, legs) or face; ipsilateral or contralateral to the lesion; and specific information loss).

                  Deficit: Contralateral loss of fine motor control in the hand and arm.
                  Affected area: Right hand and arm (contralateral to the left precentral gyrus).
                  Specific information loss: Difficulty with precise movements, dexterity, and coordination of the hand and arm. There will be weakness.
                    Why: The corticospinal tract controls voluntary movement on the opposite side of the body. This is because most of the fibers decussate (cross over) in the medulla. Therefore, a lesion in the left precentral gyrus (hand/arm region) would cause a deficit in the right hand and arm. The deficit would primarily involve fine motor control because this area is most involved in precise, skilled movements.

            C. Place an “x” over the descending motor pathway (CST) at the pontine level of your drawn diagram.

                  The “x” should be placed on the ventral aspect of the pons.
                    Why: The corticospinal tract descends through the brainstem, including the pons. A lesion here directly interrupts the motor signals traveling from the cortex to the spinal cord.

            D. Describe the deficit you would expect to see in your patient with the above lesion (note specifics such as body (arm, trunk, legs) or face; ipsilateral or contralateral to the lesion; and specific information loss).

                  Deficit: Contralateral hemiparesis (weakness) or hemiplegia (paralysis).
                  Affected area: Right side of the body (arm, trunk, leg). The face may also be involved depending on the extent of the lesion.
                  Specific information loss: Loss of voluntary motor control, weakness, spasticity, and possibly exaggerated reflexes.
                    Why: At the pontine level, the corticospinal tract fibers are still on their way to the pyramidal decussation in the medulla. This is still before the decussation occurs, so it results in a contralateral deficit. The deficit is more widespread because a larger portion of the motor fibers are affected.

                    Because a significant portion of the corticospinal tract is affected.

            E. Place an “x” over the descending motor pathway (Lateral CST) located within the dorsolateral white matter of the cervical spinal cord.

                  The "x" should be placed on the left dorsolateral white matter of the cervical spinal cord
                    Why: The lateral corticospinal tract, which has decussated in the medulla, descends in the dorsolateral white matter of the spinal cord. This tract primarily controls limb movements. At the cervical level, it contains fibers that will innervate the upper and lower extremities.

            F. Describe the deficit you would expect to see in your patient with the above lesion (note specifics such as body (arm, trunk, legs) or face; ipsilateral or contralateral to the lesion; and specific information loss).

                  Deficit: Ipsilateral weakness (paresis) or paralysis (plegia) of the upper and lower extremity.
                  Affected area: Left side of the body (arm and leg).
                  Specific information loss: Loss of voluntary motor control, weakness, spasticity, and possibly exaggerated reflexes.
                    Why: After decussation in the medulla, the lateral corticospinal tract descends ipsilaterally in the spinal cord. The lesion therefore causes motor deficits on the same side of the body.

                    Since the lateral corticospinal tract is the primary motor pathway for controlling limb movement (especially skilled and voluntary movement)

            2. What other signs would you expect to observe in a patient with a UMN lesion?

               Hyperreflexia (exaggerated reflexes)
               Clonus (rhythmic, involuntary muscle contractions)
               Positive Babinski sign (extension of the big toe and fanning of the other toes in response to stroking the lateral sole of the foot)
               Spasticity

            3. Define hypertonia and then describe the difference between spasticity and rigidity.

               Hypertonia: Increased muscle tone or resistance to passive movement.
               Spasticity: A velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone caused by hyperexcitability of the stretch reflex. Resistance to passive movement increases with increasing speed of stretch.
               Rigidity: Increased muscle tone that is not velocity-dependent and is present throughout the range of motion. It is often described as "lead-pipe" or "cogwheel" resistance.
                    ¦cogwheel = coge el volante = curiosament, encara que va de cotches, no va de velocitat

            5. Describe the different components of the motor cortex and what deficits you may see if there was a lesion to each area.

               Primary Motor Cortex (Precentral Gyrus):
                   Function: Execution of voluntary movements.
                   Deficits: Contralateral weakness or paralysis (hemiparesis or hemiplegia), loss of fine motor control, and difficulty with precise movements.
               Premotor Cortex (Anterior to Precentral Gyrus):
                   Function: Planning and sequencing of movements; selection of appropriate motor plans.
                   Deficits: Difficulty with motor planning and sequencing, apraxia (inability to perform learned movements on command), and impaired coordination of complex movements.
               Supplementary Motor Area (SMA) (Medial aspect of the frontal lobe):
                   Function: Planning and initiation of self-generated movements; coordinating bilateral movements.
                   Deficits: Difficulty initiating movements, impaired coordination of bilateral movements, and akinetic mutism (in severe cases).

            6. Your patient has had a lesion to the medial aspect of the left pons. Please answer the following questions regarding their case.

            A. Which blood supply structures were likely affected to cause damage to the medial pons?

                  Basilar artery branches (pontine arteries).
                    Why: The medial pons is primarily supplied by branches of the basilar artery, specifically the pontine arteries. Occlusion or damage to these vessels would lead to ischemia and infarction of the medial pontine structures.

            B. Are either of the 2 major ascending sensory tracts involved? If so, what information is lost from what part of the body?

                  Medial lemniscus: Involved. Loss of fine touch, vibration, and proprioception from the contralateral (right) side of the body.
                  Spinothalamic tract: Can be involved, resulting in loss of pain and temperature from the contralateral (right) side of the body.
                    Why:

                    Medial lemniscus: Ascends through the medial pons, carrying fine touch, vibration, and proprioceptive information. A lesion would disrupt this tract, resulting in contralateral sensory loss.

                    Spinothalamic tract: Although it ascends more laterally, it could be involved in an extensive medial pontine lesion.

                    The sensory information lost would be from the right side of the body.

            C. Is an ascending cerebellar pathway involved? If so, which tracts and what information is lost from what part of the body?

                  Yes, the pontocerebellar fibers which originate from the pontine nuclei and decussate to enter the contralateral middle cerebellar peduncle would be affected. This would lead to incoordination on the ipsilateral (left) side due to the cerebellum's influence on the same side of the body.
                    Why: Pontine nuclei are in the pons, and the pontocerebellar fibers are axons from pontine nuclei that cross the midline and contribute to the middle cerebellar peduncle. The cerebellum influences motor coordination on the ipsilateral side. Lesion interrupts the signal and creates incoordination ipsilateral to the injury.

            D. Are any descending cortical motor pathways involved? If so, identify the tracts involved, the movement performance deficit, and the area of the body.

                  Corticospinal tract: Involved. Weakness or paralysis of the contralateral (right) side of the body.
                  Corticobulbar tract: Involved. Weakness of the contralateral lower face.
                    Why: The corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts descend through the ventral pons, carrying motor commands. The corticospinal tract controls voluntary movement of the limbs, while the corticobulbar tract controls muscles of the face, head, and neck through the cranial nerves.

                    The right side is affected.

            E. Are there any cranial nerves or related structures involved? If so, identify the structures involved and related deficits.

                  Abducens nerve (CN VI): May be involved. Ipsilateral (left) lateral rectus muscle paralysis, leading to impaired abduction (outward movement) of the left eye.
                    Why: The abducens nucleus (CN VI) is located in the caudal pons and the facial nerve (VII) nucleus is in the caudal pons. A lesion in the medial pons affects nerve fibers as they leave their nuclei.

            F. Given the structures that are involved, what do you expect to find on your neurologic exam and interaction with the patient? What systems would you expect to be intact?

                  Expected findings:
                   Contralateral hemiparesis (right side).
                   Contralateral sensory loss (right side – touch, vibration, proprioception).
                   Ipsilateral (left) abducens nerve palsy (impaired eye abduction).
                   Possible incoordination on the left side.
                        Why: The combination of motor, sensory, and cerebellar pathway involvement would lead to a specific pattern of deficits that can be predicted based on the anatomy of the pons. This pattern helps localize the lesion to the medial pons.

                        Intact Systems: Structures and pathways outside the medial pons, such as vision and cognition could be intact (depending on the spread of the lesions).

            7. Your next patient has a lesion that affects the ventromedial aspect of the right midbrain. Please answer the following questions regarding their case.

            A. Are either of the 2 major ascending sensory tracts involved? If so, what information is lost from what part of the body?

               Yes, the medial lemniscus and spinothalamic tract are likely involved. This would result in contralateral (left) loss of fine touch, vibration, proprioception (medial lemniscus), and pain and temperature sensation (spinothalamic tract) from the left side of the body.
                    Why:

                    Medial lemniscus: Ascends through the midbrain. As the lemniscus ascends it rotates dorsal-laterally, so more laterally placed than the spinothalamic. A lesion in this area would disrupt the medial lemniscus, resulting in contralateral sensory loss.

                    Spinothalamic tract: Also ascends through the midbrain.

                    The information lost is fine touch, vibration, and proprioception from the left (contralateral) side of the body.

            B. Is an ascending cerebellar pathway structure involved? If so, what information is lost from what part of the body?

               Potentially the superior cerebellar peduncle. This would disrupt cerebellar outflow, leading to incoordination, ataxia, and tremor primarily on the ipsilateral (right) side of the body.
                    Why: The superior cerebellar peduncle decussates in the midbrain. A lesion would disrupt cerebellar outflow, leading to incoordination, ataxia, and tremor primarily on the ipsilateral (right) side of the body.

            C. Are any descending cortical motor pathways involved? If so, identify the tracts involved, the movement performance deficit, and the area of the body.

               The corticospinal tract is likely involved as it passes through the cerebral peduncles in the midbrain. This would cause contralateral (left) weakness or paralysis in the arm, leg, and possibly lower face.
                    Why: Corticospinal tract is involved as it passes through the cerebral peduncles in the midbrain. This is before decussation has occurred. This would cause contralateral (left) weakness or paralysis in the arm, leg, and potentially lower face.

            D. Are there any cranial nerves or related structures involved? If so, identify the structures involved and related deficits.

               Oculomotor nerve (CN III): May be involved. Ipsilateral (right) oculomotor nerve palsy, causing ptosis (drooping eyelid), mydriasis (pupil dilation), and impaired eye movements (difficulty with adduction, elevation, and depression of the right eye).
                    Why: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) exits the midbrain ventrally. A lesion affects the nerve or the nucleus. There is a resulting ipsilateral (right) oculomotor nerve palsy.

            E. Given the structures that are involved, what do you expect to find on your neurologic exam? What systems would you expect to be intact?

               Expected Findings:
                   Contralateral (left) hemiparesis (weakness).
                   Contralateral (left) sensory loss (touch, vibration, proprioception, pain, temperature).
                   Ipsilateral (right) oculomotor nerve palsy (CN III).
                   Potential for ipsilateral ataxia.
                        Why: The combination of sensory, motor, and cerebellar pathway involvement leads to a specific pattern of deficits depending on the structures affected in the midbrain.

    RUPERTA ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
        Case Scenario - Case-based Learning  
            Larry was throwing javelins with his sister one sunny afternoon in the park. While Larry ran to grab water, his sister accidentally threw one at him. It cut through the left half of his spinal cord at C5.

            Instructions:  
                1. On the template of the nervous system below:  
                   - Draw the pathways indicated.  
                   - Indicate with an “X” where the lesion has occurred for the patient (left half of the spinal cord at C5).  
                2. Answer the following questions based on the case scenario.

            Questions:
                1. What is the direction in which this tract carries information?  
                - Answer:  
                  b. Descending  
                    Rationale: The lateral corticospinal tract (CST) is a descending motor pathway that originates in the cerebral cortex and terminates on motor neurons in the spinal cord. It transmits voluntary motor commands from the brain to the muscles.

                2. What is the general type of information carried by this tract?  
                - Answer:  
                  a. Motor  
                    Rationale: The lateral CST is responsible for carrying motor commands for voluntary movement, particularly fine motor control of the limbs.

                3. What functions/abilities will the patient lose below C5, from this tract?  
                - Answer:  
                  Below C5, Larry will lose voluntary motor control of muscles innervated by the lateral corticospinal tract. Specifically:  
                  - Loss of fine motor control of the limbs (e.g., hand dexterity, finger movements).  
                  - Weakness or paralysis of voluntary movements in the limbs.  
                  - Impaired ability to perform coordinated and fractionated movements (e.g., reaching, grasping, buttoning a shirt).  

                  Rationale: The lateral CST primarily controls distal limb muscles, especially those involved in skilled, precise movements. A lesion at C5 disrupts these descending motor commands, leading to deficits in voluntary motor function below the level of the lesion.

                4. On which side of the body will the patient lose those functions/abilities?  
                - Answer:  
                  The patient will lose motor functions on the right side of the body.  

                  Rationale: The lateral corticospinal tract crosses over (decussates) at the pyramidal decussation in the medulla oblongata. Therefore, fibers originating in the left motor cortex travel down the spinal cord on the right side. A lesion to the left half of the spinal cord at C5 will affect the lateral CST fibers traveling to the right side of the body, resulting in motor deficits on the contralateral (right) side.

            Lateral Corticospinal Tract Diagram:
                A. Cortical/BS Template  
                    Label each of the following:  
                    1. Pre-central gyrus (face, arms, trunk, legs):  
                       - The origin of the lateral CST.  
                       - Represented somatotopically, with the face located laterally and the leg medially.  

                    2. Internal capsule:  
                       - The tract passes through the posterior limb of the internal capsule as it descends from the cortex.  

                    3. Midbrain/cerebral peduncle:  
                       - The tract travels through the ventral midbrain (cerebral peduncles).  

                    4. Pons, medulla, 3-levels of SC:  
                       - The tract continues through the pons and medulla, then crosses over at the pyramidal decussation before entering the spinal cord.  

                    5. Descending axon, from origin to termination at SC (include level of crossing):  
                       - Axons descend from the pre-central gyrus, pass through the internal capsule, cerebral peduncles, pons, and medulla. At the pyramidal decussation, 90% of the fibers cross to the contralateral side and descend in the lateral funiculus of the spinal cord.  

                B. Spinal Cord Template  
                    Draw and label each of the following:  
                    1. Medial and Lateral MN—INT's:  
                       - Medial motor neurons and interneurons: Innervate axial and proximal muscles (not significantly affected in this case).  
                       - Lateral motor neurons and interneurons: Innervate distal limb muscles (affected by the lesion).  

                    2. Lateral CST (white matter bundle):  
                       - Located in the dorsolateral white matter of the spinal cord.  
                       - Mark an "X" at the level of C5 on the left side to indicate the lesion.  

                    3. Axon termination on Lateral MN-INT's:  
                       - The lateral CST axons terminate on lateral motor neurons and interneurons in the ventral horn gray matter.  
                       - These connections are disrupted below C5 due to the lesion, leading to motor deficits on the contralateral (right) side of the body.

            Summary of Findings:  
                - Lesion Location: Left half of the spinal cord at C5.  
                - Affected Tract: Lateral corticospinal tract.  
                - Deficits:  
                  - Loss of voluntary motor control of the right limbs below C5.  
                  - Impaired fine motor skills and coordination on the right side.  
                  - No sensory deficits from the lateral CST (as it is purely motor).  

            This case highlights the importance of the lateral corticospinal tract in controlling skilled, voluntary movements and the impact of spinal cord lesions on motor function.

    .('34 PT2060_Mod7_Cerebellum - Cellular Anatomy PDF.pdf')
        .To Be Covered

        .Main Functions
            Question 1:  
            Which of the following is NOT a primary function of the cerebellum?  
            a) Regulation of autonomic functions such as heart rate and digestion  
            b) Maintenance of posture and balance  
            c) Coordination of voluntary motor activity  
            d) Assistance in motor planning  

            Correct Answer: a) Regulation of autonomic functions such as heart rate and digestion  

            Rationale: The cerebellum is primarily involved in motor-related functions, including the maintenance of posture, balance, muscle tone, coordination of voluntary movements, and assistance in motor planning. It also plays a role in cognition, particularly in tasks that require timing and attention. However, regulation of autonomic functions like heart rate and digestion is primarily controlled by the brainstem and hypothalamus, not the cerebellum.  

            - b) Maintenance of posture and balance is a key function of the cerebellum, especially through its connections with the vestibular system.  
            - c) Coordination of voluntary motor activity is central to the cerebellum's role, ensuring smooth and precise movements.  
            - d) Assistance in motor planning involves the cerebellum's interaction with the cerebral cortex to prepare and execute planned movements.

            ---

            Question 2:  
            What role does the cerebellum play in motor planning?  
            a) It directly initiates motor commands to the muscles  
            b) It assists in the preparation and execution of planned movements  
            c) It regulates involuntary reflexes without cortical input  
            d) It processes sensory information for autonomic responses  

            Correct Answer: b) It assists in the preparation and execution of planned movements  

            Rationale: The cerebellum plays a crucial role in motor planning by assisting the cerebral cortex in preparing and executing planned movements. It integrates sensory input and motor commands to ensure that movements are smooth, coordinated, and executed with appropriate timing. The cerebellum does not directly initiate motor commands (a), regulate involuntary reflexes (c), or process sensory information for autonomic responses (d).  

            - a) Direct initiation of motor commands is handled by the motor cortex and other descending pathways, not the cerebellum.  
            - c) Regulation of involuntary reflexes is more associated with the spinal cord and brainstem.  
            - d) Processing sensory information for autonomic responses is primarily the role of the hypothalamus and brainstem.

            ---

            Question 3:  
            True or False: The cerebellum has no role in cognitive functions and is solely involved in motor control.  

            Correct Answer: False  

            Rationale: While the cerebellum is primarily known for its role in motor control, it also contributes to cognitive functions. Research has shown that the cerebellum is involved in tasks requiring attention, language, and even emotional regulation. This involvement in cognition is thought to be due to its connections with the cerebral cortex, particularly in areas related to executive function and working memory. Therefore, the statement that the cerebellum is solely involved in motor control is incorrect.  

            - Complementary Information: Cognitive impairments have been observed in patients with cerebellar damage, further supporting the cerebellum's role in non-motor functions.

            ---

            Question 4:  
            Which of the following best describes the cerebellum's role in maintaining muscle tone?  
            a) It directly stimulates muscle contractions through motor neurons  
            b) It modulates the activity of motor neurons to maintain appropriate muscle tone  
            c) It inhibits excessive muscle contractions to prevent spasticity  
            d) It regulates muscle tone through direct connections with the basal ganglia  

            Correct Answer: b) It modulates the activity of motor neurons to maintain appropriate muscle tone  

            Rationale: The cerebellum helps maintain muscle tone by modulating the activity of motor neurons, ensuring that muscles are neither too relaxed nor too tense. It does this by integrating sensory feedback and adjusting motor output accordingly. The cerebellum does not directly stimulate muscle contractions (a), inhibit excessive contractions (c), or regulate muscle tone through the basal ganglia (d).  

            - a) Direct stimulation of muscle contractions is the role of alpha motor neurons in the spinal cord.  
            - c) Inhibition of excessive contractions is more closely associated with the role of inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord.  
            - d) The basal ganglia are involved in regulating movement initiation and inhibition but do not directly interact with the cerebellum for muscle tone regulation.

            ---

            Question 5:  
            How does the cerebellum contribute to balance and posture?  
            a) By directly controlling skeletal muscles through the corticospinal tract  
            b) By integrating sensory input from the vestibular system and proprioceptive feedback  
            c) By regulating blood pressure and heart rate to maintain equilibrium  
            d) By modulating the release of neurotransmitters in the motor cortex  

            Correct Answer: b) By integrating sensory input from the vestibular system and proprioceptive feedback  

            Rationale: The cerebellum contributes to balance and posture by integrating sensory input from the vestibular system (which detects changes in head position and motion) and proprioceptive feedback (which provides information about body position and movement). This integration allows the cerebellum to make real-time adjustments to maintain balance and posture. The cerebellum does not directly control skeletal muscles via the corticospinal tract (a), regulate blood pressure or heart rate (c), or modulate neurotransmitter release in the motor cortex (d).  

            - a) The corticospinal tract is responsible for voluntary motor control, not balance and posture regulation.  
            - c) Blood pressure and heart rate regulation are functions of the autonomic nervous system, not the cerebellum.  
            - d) Neurotransmitter modulation in the motor cortex is more related to motor planning and execution, not balance.

            ---

            Question 6:  
            True or False: The cerebellum's role in cognition is limited to motor-related cognitive tasks such as timing and attention.  

            Correct Answer: False  

            Rationale: While the cerebellum is indeed involved in motor-related cognitive tasks such as timing and attention, its role in cognition extends beyond these functions. Research has shown that the cerebellum is also involved in higher-order cognitive processes, including language processing, emotional regulation, and even decision-making. These cognitive functions are thought to arise from the cerebellum's extensive connections with the cerebral cortex, particularly in areas involved in executive function.  

            - Complementary Information: Damage to the cerebellum can lead to cognitive deficits in areas such as language and emotional processing, indicating its broader role in cognition.

            Question 1:
            Which of the following best describes the role of the cerebellum in motor control?  
            a) It directly initiates motor commands to the muscles  
            b) It modulates motor output by detecting and correcting errors during movement  
            c) It regulates autonomic functions such as heart rate and digestion  
            d) It processes sensory information for emotional responses  

            Correct Answer: b) It modulates motor output by detecting and correcting errors during movement  

            Rationale: The cerebellum plays a critical role in motor control by detecting discrepancies (errors) between intended movements and actual performance. It does not directly initiate motor commands (a), regulate autonomic functions (c), or process sensory information for emotional responses (d). Instead, it refines motor output through feedback loops that adjust muscle activity and ensure smooth, coordinated movements.  

            - a) Direct initiation of motor commands is handled by the motor cortex and descending pathways like the corticospinal tract.  
            - c) Autonomic regulation is primarily managed by the hypothalamus and brainstem.  
            - d) Emotional processing involves structures like the amygdala and prefrontal cortex, not the cerebellum.

It does not serve as an input pathway (a), regulate balance exclusively (c), or store long-term memories (d).

            Question 3:  
            True or False: Mossy fibers synapse directly on Purkinje cells to influence motor coordination.  

            Correct Answer: False  

            Rationale: Mossy fibers do not synapse directly on Purkinje cells. Instead, they synapse on granule cells, which then send parallel fibers to excite Purkinje cells. This indirect pathway allows for the integration of sensory and motor information before reaching the output neurons of the cerebellum.  

            - Complementary Information: Climbing fibers, in contrast, synapse directly on Purkinje cells and play a critical role in signaling movement errors.

            Question 2: 
            What type of synapse do Purkinje cells form with deep cerebellar nuclei and vestibular nuclei?  
            a) Excitatory synapses  
            b) Inhibitory synapses  
            c) Modulatory synapses  
            d) Neutral synapses  

            Correct Answer: b) Inhibitory synapses ¦Droga

            Rationale: Purkinje cells form inhibitory synapses on deep cerebellar nuclei and vestibular nuclei. This inhibition is crucial for modulating the output of the cerebellum, allowing for precise control of motor movements and coordination.

            - a) Purkinje cells do not form excitatory synapses; their primary role is to inhibit the activity of deep cerebellar nuclei.  
            - c) While Purkinje cells play a role in modulating motor output, their primary mechanism is through inhibitory synapses.  
            - d) There is no such thing as a "neutral synapse" in this context.

            ---

            Question 3: (!!F) 
            Which cells are excited by parallel fibers and terminate on Purkinje cell bodies?  
            a) Stellate cells  
            b) Basket cells  
            c) Golgi cells  
            d) Granule cells  

            Correct Answer: b) Basket cells  

            Rationale: Basket cells are inhibitory interneurons (perque són jugadors paraplègics) that are excited by parallel fibers (entrenen en barres para.leles = excitatory) and terminate on Purkinje cell bodies. They play a role in regulating the firing rate of Purkinje cells, contributing to the precise timing and coordination of cerebellar output.
                ¦"timing and coordination" es molt important, per part del equip de basket, per a clavar la pilota en el basket, guanyar, i anarse'n al intemig (interneurons) que es lo divertit en el partit de basket (perque aixina veuen a les animadores ballar?). Tota eixa energia de voler anar el intermig, es arreplegà per Pumuki alquimicament (un altre ingredient de la poció), en el bosc del costat del estadi, per a fer la poció que es inhibitòria 

            - a) Stellate cells are also inhibitory interneurons, but they terminate on Purkinje cell dendrites, not cell bodies.  
            - c) Golgi cells are excited by parallel fibers but provide feedback inhibition onto granule cell dendrites, not Purkinje cell bodies.  
            - d) Granule cells form parallel fibers and excite Purkinje cells but do not terminate on Purkinje cell bodies.

            Which cells provide feedback inhibition onto granule cell dendrites?

            Rationale: Golgi cells are excited by parallel fibers and provide feedback inhibition onto granule cell dendrites. This feedback loop helps regulate the excitation of granule cells, ensuring that the cerebellar circuitry functions smoothly.

            - a) Basket cells terminate on Purkinje cell bodies and do not provide feedback inhibition onto granule cells.  
            - b) Stellate cells terminate on Purkinje cell dendrites and do not interact with granule cells.  
            - d) Purkinje cells are the main output neurons of the cerebellar cortex and do not provide feedback inhibition onto granule cells.

            Question 5:  
            True or False: Granule cells form parallel fibers that make excitatory contacts with numerous Purkinje cells.  

            Correct Answer: True
                ¦Granule (els mensatges en les pedres) comunica amb Pumiki, no Mossy directament

            Rationale: Granule cells bifurcate to form parallel fibers, which run parallel to the surface of the cerebellar cortex. These parallel fibers form excitatory contacts with numerous Purkinje cells, allowing for widespread integration of sensory and motor information within the cerebellar circuitry.

            - Complementary Information: The excitatory input from parallel fibers is essential for activating Purkinje cells, which then modulate the output of the cerebellum through inhibitory synapses on deep cerebellar nuclei.

        .Cerebellar Peduncles
            Question 1: (!!F)
            Which cerebellar peduncle primarily receives afferents from the spinal cerebellar tracts, medulla, and vestibular nuclei?  
            a) Superior cerebellar peduncle  
            b) Middle cerebellar peduncle  
            c) Inferior cerebellar peduncle  

            Correct Answer: c) Inferior cerebellar peduncle  

            Rationale: The inferior cerebellar peduncle (ICP) is responsible for receiving afferent information from the spinal cerebellar tracts, medulla, and vestibular nuclei. It also sends efferent information back to the vestibular nuclei, playing a key role in balance and coordination.
                ¦Pensa amb un triangle o una piramide = tècnica de la estabilitat = base = Inferior cerebellar peduncle = balance and coordination (on va balance va sempre coordination?) = E clava les puntes en terra per a estabilitzar

            - a) The superior cerebellar peduncle (SCP) is primarily an output pathway, sending efferent information to the diencephalon, brainstem, and cortex.  
            - b) The middle cerebellar peduncle (MCP) primarily receives afferents from the pons via pontocerebellar fibers, not directly from the spinal cord or vestibular nuclei.

            ---

            Question 2:  
            Which cerebellar peduncle is primarily responsible for sending efferent information to the diencephalon, brainstem, and cortex?  
            a) Inferior cerebellar peduncle  
            b) Middle cerebellar peduncle  
            c) Superior cerebellar peduncle  

            Correct Answer: c) Superior cerebellar peduncle  

            Rationale: The superior cerebellar peduncle (SCP) is the primary output pathway of the cerebellum, sending efferent information to the diencephalon, brainstem, and cortex. This pathway is crucial for transmitting processed motor and sensory information to higher brain centers for further integration and execution.

            - a) The inferior cerebellar peduncle (ICP) primarily receives afferent information and sends efferents back to the vestibular nuclei, not to the diencephalon or cortex.  
            - b) The middle cerebellar peduncle (MCP) is mainly an input pathway, receiving afferents from the pons via pontocerebellar fibers.

            ---

            Question 3:  
            True or False: The middle cerebellar peduncle primarily carries afferent information from the pons to the cerebellum.  

            Correct Answer: True  

            Rationale: The middle cerebellar peduncle (MCP) primarily carries afferent information from the pons to the cerebellum. These afferents are part of the pontocerebellar fibers, which convey motor-related information from the cerebral cortex to the cerebellum via the pontine nuclei. This pathway is essential for motor planning and coordination.

            Question 5:  
            What is the primary function of the inferior cerebellar peduncle?  
            a) Transmitting afferent information from the spinal cord to the spinocerebellum  
            b) Conveying efferent information from the cerebrocerebellum to the thalamus  
            c) Carrying afferents from the cerebral cortex to the pontine nuclei

            Rationale: The inferior cerebellar peduncle (ICP) primarily transmits afferent information from the spinal cord to the spinocerebellum. This includes inputs from the dorsal spinocerebellar and cuneocerebellar tracts, as well as vestibular nuclei, which are essential for maintaining balance and coordinating movements.

        .Cerebellar Inputs
            Question 1: (!!F)
            Which input pathway carries proprioceptive information from the legs and synapses in the nucleus dorsalis of Clarke before reaching the cerebellum? 

            a) Ventral spinocerebellar tract
            b) Dorsal spinocerebellar tract
            c) Rubrospinal tract
            d) Corticospinal tract 

            Correct Answer: Dorsal spinocerebellar tract  

            Rationale: The dorsal spinocerebellar tract originates from leg proprioceptors and synapses in the nucleus dorsalis of Clarke, which is located in the spinal cord. This pathway then transmits non-conscious proprioceptive information to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
                -¦Clarke es el nom del traballaor que pasa per ahí, que es un egoista (proprioceptors) i inconcient (non-conscious) perque va al vestíbul de les putes també 

            ---

            Question 2: (!!F)
            Which cerebellar peduncle primarily carries input from the pontine nuclei, which receive motor-related information from the cerebral cortex?

            a) Superior cerebellar peduncle
            b) Middle cerebellar peduncle
            c) Inferior cerebellar peduncle
            d) Medial cerebellar peduncle

            Correct Answer: Middle cerebellar peduncle  

            Rationale: The middle cerebellar peduncle is the primary pathway for pontocerebellar fibers. These fibers originate in the cerebral cortex, project to the pontine nuclei in the brainstem, and then travel to the cerebellum, carrying motor-related information.

            ---

            Question 3: (!!F)
            True or False: The ventral spinocerebellar tract carries information about whole-body movement and travels through the superior cerebellar peduncle.

            a) True
            b) False

            Correct Answer: True  

            Rationale: The ventral spinocerebellar tract carries non-conscious proprioceptive information about whole-body movement or inter-limb coordination. Unlike other spinocerebellar tracts, it ascends through the superior cerebellar peduncle after crossing at the level of the spinal cord or pons.

            ---

            Question 4: (!!F)
            Which input pathway originates from the vestibular system and projects to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle?

            a) Vestibular inputs
            b) Spinothalamic tract
            c) Dorsal column-medial lemniscal system
            d) Reticulospinal tract

            Correct Answer: Vestibular inputs  

            Rationale: Vestibular inputs originate from the vestibular system (e.g., vestibular ganglia and nuclei) and carry information related to balance, head position, and spatial orientation. These inputs reach the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
                ¦Vestibular inputs = Vestibular system

            ---

            Question 5:
            Which cells in the brainstem project climbing fibers to the cerebellum, and through which cerebellar peduncle do these fibers travel?  

            a) Red nucleus; middle cerebellar peduncle
            b) Inferior olivary nucleus; inferior cerebellar peduncle
            c) Pontine nuclei; middle cerebellar peduncle
            d) Dentate nucleus; superior cerebellar peduncle

            Correct Answer: Inferior olivary nucleus; inferior cerebellar peduncle
                ¦Climbing = de Oliva = escalen desde el sótona, no la planta baixa

            Rationale: Climbing fibers originate from the inferior olivary nucleus in the medulla oblongata and project to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle. These fibers play a crucial role in signaling errors in movement and facilitating motor learning.

        .Cerebellar Outputs
            Question 1:  
            Which cerebellar region is primarily responsible for motor planning of the extremities, and through which cerebellar peduncle does this information leave?

            a) Intermediate hemispheres; inferior cerebellar peduncle
            b) Flocculonodular lobe; inferior cerebellar peduncle
            c) Lateral hemispheres; superior cerebellar peduncle
            d) Vermis; middle cerebellar peduncle  

            Correct Answer:  
            Lateral hemispheres; superior cerebellar peduncle
                ¦

                    -Lo únic que entra es el superior cerebellar peduncle
                    -I dentate nucleus, per ser el més llarg, arriba hasta els extrems, per lo que està rel.lacionat ahí

            Rationale:  
            The lateral hemispheres of the cerebellum are associated with the dentate nucleus and are responsible for motor planning of the extremities. This information leaves the cerebellum via the superior cerebellar peduncle and influences the lateral corticospinal tract, which is crucial for executing skilled voluntary movements.  

            - Incorrect Option 1: Intermediate hemispheres; inferior cerebellar peduncle – The intermediate hemispheres are involved in distal limb coordination, not motor planning, and their output travels via the superior cerebellar peduncle, not the inferior.  
            - Incorrect Option 2: Vermis; middle cerebellar peduncle – The vermis is responsible for proximal limb and trunk coordination, not motor planning, and its output travels via both the superior and inferior cerebellar peduncles, not the middle.  
            - Incorrect Option 3: Flocculonodular lobe; inferior cerebellar peduncle – The flocculonodular lobe is involved in balance and vestibulo-ocular reflexes, not motor planning, and its output travels via the inferior cerebellar peduncle but does not influence the lateral corticospinal tract.

        .Functional Divisions
            Question 1:  
            Which functional division of the cerebellum is primarily associated with connections to the vestibular system and is responsible for balance and eye movements?

            Spinocerebellum
            Cerebrocerebellum
            vestibulocerebellum  

            Correct Answer:  
            Vestibulocerebellum 

            Rationale:  
            The vestibulocerebellum, shown in purple, is primarily associated with the vestibular system. It plays a key role in maintaining balance, coordinating eye movements, and stabilizing gaze during head movements. This division receives input from the vestibular apparatus and sends output to the vestibular nuclei in the brainstem, influencing both balance and equilibrium as well as eye movement control.  

            - Incorrect Option 1: Spinocerebellum – The spinocerebellum (shown in blue) is connected to the spinal cord and is involved in motor coordination, particularly in the execution of ongoing movements and the regulation of muscle tone. It does not directly interact with the vestibular system.
                ¦Spino = Puerco Spino = Sonic que pensa poc i força bruta = Motor execution of ongoing movements and the regulation of muscle tone
            - Incorrect Option 2: Cerebrocerebellum – The cerebrocerebellum (shown in green) has direct connections to the cerebrum and is involved in motor planning, timing, and cognitive functions. It does not have a primary role in balance or vestibular-related functions.
                ¦Es més cerebral i te característiques "motor planning, timing, and cognitive functions"; en contrast to Sonic

            ---

            Question 2: 
            True or False: The spinocerebellum is primarily involved in the execution of ongoing movements and receives inputs from the spinal cord.  

            Correct Answer: True  

            Rationale:  
            The spinocerebellum, which includes the vermis and paravermal regions, is primarily involved in the execution of ongoing movements, including the coordination of limb movements and the maintenance of posture. It receives proprioceptive inputs from the spinal cord via ascending pathways such as the spinocerebellar tracts. These inputs allow the spinocerebellum to monitor and adjust movements based on sensory feedback, ensuring smooth and coordinated motor performance.   

            ---

            Question 3:  
            Which functional division of the cerebellum has direct connections to the cerebrum?

            cerebrocerebellum
            Spinocerebellum
            Cerebrocerebellum

            Correct Answer: Cerebrocerebellum  

            Rationale:  
            The cerebrocerebellum, shown in green, has direct connections to the cerebrum and is primarily involved in motor planning, timing, and the coordination of skilled voluntary movements. It receives input from cortical areas, particularly the motor and premotor cortices, and sends output back to these areas via the thalamus. This allows the cerebrocerebellum to refine motor commands and adapt movements based on sensory feedback and cognitive strategies.  

            - Incorrect Option 1: Vestibulocerebellum – The vestibulocerebellum (purple) is associated with the vestibular system and is responsible for balance and eye movements, not direct connections to the cerebrum.  
            - Incorrect Option 2: Spinocerebellum – The spinocerebellum (blue) is connected to the spinal cord and focuses on motor execution and coordination, not direct cerebrum interactions.  

            ---

            Question 4:  
            Select all that apply: Which of the following statements about the functional divisions of the cerebellum are correct?  
            a) The vestibulocerebellum is involved in balance and eye movements.  
            b) The spinocerebellum primarily influences axial and proximal limb muscles.  
            c) The cerebrocerebellum receives input from the cerebral cortex and projects back to it.  
            d) The vestibulocerebellum uses the dentate nucleus as its primary output structure.  

            Correct Answers:  
            a) The vestibulocerebellum is involved in balance and eye movements.  
            b) The spinocerebellum primarily influences axial and proximal limb muscles.  
            c) The cerebrocerebellum receives input from the cerebral cortex and projects back to it.  

            Rationale:  
            - Correct Option a: The vestibulocerebellum is crucial for maintaining balance and coordinating eye movements in response to vestibular inputs.  
            - Correct Option b: The spinocerebellum, particularly the vermis, influences axial and proximal limb muscles through its connections with medial descending motor pathways.  
            - Correct Option c: The cerebrocerebellum receives input from the cerebral cortex, processes it, and projects back to cortical areas via the thalamus, playing a role in motor planning and execution.  

            - Incorrect Option d: The vestibulocerebellum does not use the dentate nucleus as its primary output structure; instead, it uses neurons in the vestibular nuclei. The dentate nucleus is associated with the cerebrocerebellum. (!!F)  

        .Vestibulocerebellum 
            Question 1:
            Which functional division of the cerebellum is primarily responsible for balance and eye movements, and what are its main afferent inputs?

            Spinocerebellum; vermis and intermediate hemisphere
            Cerebrocerebellum; cerebral cortex
            Flocculonodular lobe only
            Vestibulocerebellum; vestibular nerve/nuclei and visual input via mossy fibers

            Correct Answer:  
            Vestibulocerebellum; vestibular nerve/nuclei and visual input via mossy fibers
                ¦Input = Mossy amb els mensatges creen una representació visual del reigne

            Rationale:  
            The vestibulocerebellum, which includes the flocculonodular lobe and adjacent portions of the vermis, is primarily responsible for maintaining balance and coordinating eye movements. Its main afferent inputs include signals from the vestibular nerve/nuclei (which provide information about head position and motion) and visual input via mossy fibers (which assist in orienting the eyes during movement). These inputs allow the vestibulocerebellum to integrate sensory information related to spatial orientation and head movement, ensuring stability and gaze control.  

            - Incorrect Option 1: Spinocerebellum; somatosensory input – The spinocerebellum (vermis and intermediate hemisphere) receives somatosensory input and is involved in motor execution and coordination of limb movements, not balance or eye movements.  
            - Incorrect Option 2: Cerebrocerebellum; cortical input – The cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres) receives input from the cerebral cortex and is involved in motor planning and cognitive tasks, not balance or vestibular reflexes.  
            - Incorrect Option 3: Flocculonodular lobe only; auditory input – While the flocculonodular lobe is part of the vestibulocerebellum, it does not receive auditory input. Instead, it processes vestibular and visual information to maintain balance and coordinate eye movements.

            True or False: The vestibulocerebellum sends efferent outputs to the medial motor systems, including the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts, as well as the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF).  

            Correct Answer: True

            Rationale:
            The vestibulocerebellum sends processed information to the medial motor systems, specifically the vestibulospinal tract (VST), reticulospinal tract (RST), and medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF). These pathways are essential for controlling axial muscles, maintaining balance, and coordinating eye movements. For example, the MLF plays a critical role in synchronizing eye movements with head motion to stabilize gaze.

            Question 4:  
            What is the primary function of the vestibulocerebellum?

            Motor planning and execution
            Balance and eye movements
            Distal limb coordination
            Cognitive tasks

            Correct Answer:  
            Balance and eye movements (axial muscle control and vestibular reflexes) 

            Rationale:  
            The vestibulocerebellum is primarily responsible for maintaining balance and coordinating eye movements. It achieves this by processing sensory inputs from the vestibular system (head position and motion) and visual system (orienting the eyes) to generate appropriate motor responses. Specifically, it controls axial muscles through medial motor systems like the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts and mediates vestibular reflexes, such as the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR), which stabilizes gaze during head movements.  

            - Incorrect Option 1: Motor planning and execution – This is the role of the cerebrocerebellum, not the vestibulocerebellum.  
            - Incorrect Option 3: Distal limb coordination – This is the role of the spinocerebellum, particularly the intermediate hemisphere.  
            - Incorrect Option 4: Cognitive tasks – While the cerebellum has some involvement in cognition, this is not the primary function of the vestibulocerebellum.  

        .Spinocerebellum: Intermediate
            Question 1:  
            Which functional division of the cerebellum is associated with the intermediate cerebellar hemisphere, and what is its primary role in motor control?

            Vestibulocerebellum; balance and eye movements
            Cerebrocerebellum; motor planning and cognitive functions
            Spinocerebellum; motor execution in distal body parts

            Correct Answer:  
            Spinocerebellum; motor execution in distal body parts
                ¦Les cametes de Sonic corregent  

            Rationale:  
            The spinocerebellum, specifically the intermediate cerebellar hemisphere, is associated with motor execution in the distal body parts. It receives afferent information from the spinal cord via the spinocerebellar tracts, particularly related to proprioceptive input from distal body parts. This information is processed and then sent to the interposed nuclei, which project to lateral descending motor systems such as the corticospinal and rubrospinal tracts. These pathways are crucial for executing precise motor activities in the extremities, influencing both voluntary and involuntary movements by comparing the intended movement with the actual movement and making necessary adjustments.  

            - Incorrect Option 1: Vestibulocerebellum – The vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe) is primarily involved in balance and eye movements, not motor execution in the limbs.  
            - Incorrect Option 2: Cerebrocerebellum – The cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres) is involved in motor planning and cognitive functions, not the execution of motor activities in the distal body parts.  

            ---

            Question 2: (!!F)
            True or False: The interposed nuclei of the spinocerebellum send efferent outputs to the corticospinal and rubrospinal tracts to execute motor activities in the extremities.  

            Correct Answer: True  

            Rationale:  
            The interposed nuclei of the spinocerebellum receive processed information from the intermediate cerebellar hemisphere and send efferent outputs through lateral descending motor systems, including the corticospinal and rubrospinal tracts. These tracts are responsible for executing motor activities in the extremities, ensuring smooth and coordinated movements by integrating sensory feedback and adjusting motor commands.

            b) It sends efferent outputs to the interposed nuclei.
            c) Its primary function is motor execution in distal body parts.
            d) It influences voluntary but not involuntary movements.

            Correct Answers:  
            a) It receives afferent inputs from the spinal cord via spinocerebellar tracts.  
            b) It sends efferent outputs to the interposed nuclei.  
            c) Its primary function is motor execution in distal body parts.  

            Rationale:  
            - Correct Option a: The spinocerebellum receives afferent inputs from the spinal cord via the spinocerebellar tracts, which carry proprioceptive information from distal body parts.  
            - Correct Option b: Processed information from the intermediate cerebellar hemisphere is sent to the interposed nuclei, which then project to lateral descending motor systems.  
            - Correct Option c: The primary function of the spinocerebellum is motor execution in distal body parts, ensuring precise and coordinated movements.  

            - Incorrect Option d: The spinocerebellum influences both voluntary and involuntary movements by comparing actual versus intended movements and making appropriate adjustments.

            Question 4:

            Balance and posture
            Cognitive tasks
            motor activities

These tracts receive efferent outputs from the interposed nuclei of the spinocerebellum, which process proprioceptive information from the spinal cord. By integrating sensory feedback and adjusting motor commands, these pathways ensure precise and coordinated movements in the distal body parts.  

            - Incorrect Option 1: Balance and posture – These functions are primarily associated with the vestibulocerebellum and vermis, not the intermediate cerebellar hemisphere.  
            - Incorrect Option 2: Cognitive tasks – While the cerebrocerebellum is involved in cognitive functions, the spinocerebellum focuses on motor execution and coordination.  
            - Incorrect Option 4: Motor planning – Motor planning is the role of the cerebrocerebellum, not the spinocerebellum.  

        .Spinocerebellum: Vermis
            Question 1:  
            Which functional division of the cerebellum is associated with the vermis, and what is its primary role in motor control?

            Vestibulocerebellum; motor execution in axial and proximal body parts
            Cerebrocerebellum; regulation of axial and proximal motor execution
            Spinocerebellum; regulation of motor execution in axial and proximal body parts

            Correct Answer:  
            Spinocerebellum; regulation of motor execution in axial and proximal body parts  

            Rationale:  
            The spinocerebellum, specifically the vermis, is associated with the regulation of motor execution in axial and proximal body parts. It receives afferent inputs from the vestibular nuclei and nerve, visual and auditory systems, and sensory information from proximal body parts via the trigeminal nucleus and spinal cerebellar tracts. This information is processed and sent to the fastigial nucleus, which projects to medial descending systems (e.g., vestibular nuclei, reticular formation, and proximal regions of the motor cortex). These pathways are essential for executing motor activities in the trunk and making anticipatory and corrective responses to movements.  

            - Incorrect Option 1: Vestibulocerebellum – The vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe) is primarily involved in balance and eye movements, not motor execution in axial and proximal body parts.  
            - Incorrect Option 2: Cerebrocerebellum – The cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres) is involved in motor planning and cognitive tasks, not the regulation of axial and proximal motor execution.  

            ---

            Question 2:  
            True or False: The vermis sends efferent outputs to the vestibular nuclei and reticular formation to influence medial descending systems that control trunk movements.  

            Correct Answer: True  

            Rationale:  
            The vermis of the spinocerebellum sends efferent outputs via the fastigial nucleus to the vestibular nuclei and reticular formation. These projections influence medial descending systems, such as the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts, which are critical for controlling trunk movements and maintaining posture. This pathway ensures smooth and coordinated motor execution in axial and proximal body parts.  

            Question 3: (!!F)
            Select all that apply: Which of the following statements about the spinocerebellum (vermis) are correct?  
            a) It receives afferent inputs from the vestibular nuclei and nerve.  
            b) Its efferents project to the fastigial nucleus.  
            c) It influences medial descending systems to execute motor activities in the trunk.  
            d) It is involved in anticipatory and corrective responses to movements.  

            Correct Answers: All of them
            a) It receives afferent inputs from the vestibular nuclei and nerve.  
            b) Its efferents project to the fastigial nucleus.  
            c) It influences medial descending systems to execute motor activities in the trunk.  
            d) It is involved in anticipatory and corrective responses to movements.  

            Rationale:  
            - Correct Option a: The vermis receives afferent inputs from the vestibular nuclei and nerve, as well as other sensory systems (e.g., visual, auditory).  
            - Correct Option b: Processed information from the vermis is sent to the fastigial nucleus, which serves as the output nucleus for this region.  
            - Correct Option c: The fastigial nucleus projects to medial descending systems (e.g., vestibular nuclei, reticular formation), which control trunk movements and maintain posture.  
            - Correct Option d: Like the intermediate portion of the spinocerebellum, the vermis makes anticipatory and corrective responses to movements, ensuring smooth motor execution.

            Question 4:

            Fine motor control of distal limbs
            Cognitive tasks
            To execute motor activities
            Balance and eye movements

            Correct Answer:  
            To execute motor activities in the trunk and regulate axial and proximal body movements  

            Rationale:  
            The medial descending systems, influenced by the vermis of the spinocerebellum, play a crucial role in executing motor activities in the trunk and regulating axial and proximal body movements. These systems include the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts, which receive input from the fastigial nucleus and ensure smooth and coordinated motor execution in response to sensory feedback.  

            - Incorrect Option 2: Fine motor control of distal limbs – This is the role of the intermediate cerebellar hemisphere (interposed nuclei), not the vermis.  
            - Incorrect Option 3: Cognitive tasks – While the cerebrocerebellum is involved in cognitive functions, the vermis focuses on motor execution in axial and proximal body parts.  
            - Incorrect Option 4: Balance and eye movements – These functions are primarily associated with the vestibulocerebellum, not the vermis.  

        .Cerebrocerebellum – Motor Roles
            Question 1:  
            Which functional division of the cerebellum is associated with the lateral hemispheres, and what is its primary role in motor control?  

            a) Cerebrocerebellum; motor planning, initiation, and timing control
            b) Vestibulocerebellum; balance and eye movement control
            c) Spinocerebellum; motor execution and coordination of axial and proximal body parts
            d) Archicerebellum; regulation of autonomic functions

            Correct Answer:  
            a) Cerebrocerebellum; motor planning, initiation, and timing control  

            Rationale: 
            The cerebrocerebellum, specifically the lateral hemispheres, is associated with motor planning, initiation, and timing control. It receives afferent inputs from the cortex and pons via corticopontine fibers, processes this information, and sends it to the dentate nucleus, one of the deep cerebellar nuclei. From there, the information is relayed to the red nucleus in the brainstem via the superior cerebellar peduncle and to the thalamus, which projects to the premotor cortex. This pathway is crucial for planning, coordinating, and initiating voluntary movements, as well as controlling their timing.

                        -afferent inputs: cortex (viatge al centre de la terra) and pons via corticopontine fibers (motor planning = pasar per un pont)
                            -red nucleus (centre de la terra) in the brainstem (profund) via the superior cerebellar peduncle and to the thalamus, which projects to the premotor cortex

            - Incorrect Option 1: Vestibulocerebellum – The vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe) is primarily involved in balance and eye movements, not motor planning or timing.  
            - Incorrect Option 2: Spinocerebellum – The spinocerebellum (vermis and intermediate hemisphere) is involved in motor execution and coordination of axial and proximal body parts, not motor planning.  

            ---

            Correct Answer: True  

            Rationale:  
            The dentate nucleus, part of the cerebrocerebellum, sends efferent outputs via the superior cerebellar peduncle to the red nucleus in the brainstem and to the thalamus, which then projects to the premotor cortex. These pathways are essential for motor planning, coordination, initiation of voluntary movements, and timing control.

            Question 3:  
            Select all that apply: Which of the following statements about the cerebrocerebellum are correct?  
            a) It receives afferent inputs from the cortex and pons.  
            b) Its efferents project to the dentate nucleus.  
            c) It influences the red nucleus and premotor cortex.  
            d) Its primary function is motor execution in distal body parts.  

            Correct Answers:  
            a) It receives afferent inputs from the cortex and pons.  
            b) Its efferents project to the dentate nucleus.  
            c) It influences the red nucleus and premotor cortex.  

            Rationale:  
            - Correct Option a: The cerebrocerebellum receives afferent inputs from the cortex and pons via corticopontine fibers.  
            - Correct Option b: Processed information from the lateral hemispheres is sent to the dentate nucleus, which serves as the output nucleus for this region.  
            - Correct Option c: The dentate nucleus projects to the red nucleus in the brainstem and to the premotor cortex via the thalamus, influencing motor planning, coordination, and timing.  

            - Incorrect Option d: The primary function of the cerebrocerebellum is motor planning, initiation, and timing control, not motor execution in distal body parts (which is the role of the spinocerebellum).

            Question 4:  
            What is the role of the superior cerebellar peduncle in the context of the cerebrocerebellum's function?

            a) To relay efferent outputs
            b) To regulate balance and posture
            c) To execute motor commands in distal body parts
            d) To process cognitive tasks unrelated to motor control  

            Correct Answer:  
            To relay efferent outputs from the dentate nucleus to the red nucleus and thalamus for motor planning and timing  

            Rationale:  
            The superior cerebellar peduncle serves as the primary output pathway of the cerebrocerebellum. It relays efferent outputs from the dentate nucleus to the red nucleus in the brainstem and to the thalamus, which then projects to the premotor cortex. This pathway is critical for motor planning, coordination, initiation of voluntary movements, and timing control.  

            - Incorrect Option 1: Balance and posture – These functions are associated with the vestibulocerebellum and spinocerebellum, not the cerebrocerebellum.  
            - Incorrect Option 2: Motor execution – Motor execution in distal body parts is the role of the spinocerebellum, not the cerebrocerebellum.  
            - Incorrect Option 3: Cognitive tasks – While the cerebrocerebellum may have some cognitive roles, its primary function is motor planning and timing.

        .Cerebellar Dysfunction
            Question 1: (!!F)
            What is the hallmark movement disorder associated with cerebellar lesions, and how does it manifest?

            Spasticity; characterized by increased muscle tone and stiffness.
            Ataxia; characterized by jerky or inaccurate movements
            Bradykinesia; characterized by slowness of movement.
            Tremor; characterized by involuntary shaking or trembling.

            Correct Answer:  
            Ataxia; characterized by jerky or inaccurate movements that are not due to weakness, spasticity, or contracture.  

            Rationale:  
            Ataxia is the hallmark movement disorder of cerebellar dysfunction. It manifests as impaired coordination, resulting in jerky, uncoordinated, or inaccurate movements. This occurs because the cerebellum plays a critical role in motor coordination, timing, and error correction. Ataxia is not caused by muscle weakness, spasticity, or contracture but rather by the loss of precise control over voluntary movements.  

            ---

            Question 2:  
            True or False: All cerebellar lesions result in unilateral deficits due to the crossing of cerebral tracts before reaching the cerebellum.  

            Correct Answer: True  

            Rationale:  
            Cerebellar lesions cause unilateral deficits because the cerebellum processes information ipsilaterally (on the same side). Cerebral tracts cross prior to reaching the cerebellum, and cerebellar efferents remain ipsilateral as they project to the medial and spinocerebellar tracts. This anatomical arrangement ensures that damage to one side of the cerebellum results in deficits on the same side of the body.  

            ---

            Question 3: (!!F)
            Select all that apply: Which of the following are common manifestations of cerebellar dysfunction?  
            a) Dysarthria  
            b) Dysmetria  
            c) Spasticity  
            d) Ataxia  

            Correct Answers:  
            a) Dysarthria  
            b) Dysmetria  
            d) Ataxia  

            Rationale:  
            - Correct Option a: Dysarthria (slurred or poorly articulated speech) is a common manifestation of cerebellar dysfunction, particularly with lesions affecting the cerebrocerebellum or spinocerebellum.  
            - Correct Option b: Dysmetria (inability to accurately gauge the distance or range of movements) is another hallmark of cerebellar dysfunction.  
            - Correct Option d: Ataxia (impaired coordination) is the most common movement disorder associated with cerebellar lesions.  

            - Incorrect Option c: Spasticity is not a feature of cerebellar dysfunction; it is typically associated with upper motor neuron lesions.  

            ---

            Question 4:  
            What specific deficits are associated with lesions to the vestibulocerebellum?

            Dysdiadochokinesia, dysmetria, and action tremors.
            Spasticity, hypertonia, and clonus.
            Bradykinesia, rigidity, and postural instability.
            Nystagmus, balance impairments, and truncal ataxia.

            Correct Answer:  
            Nystagmus, balance impairments, and truncal ataxia.  

            Rationale:  
            The vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe) is responsible for maintaining balance, equilibrium, and coordinating eye movements. Lesions to this area can result in:  
            - Nystagmus (abnormal involuntary eye movements),  
            - Balance impairments, and  
            - Truncal ataxia (unsteadiness of the trunk, making it difficult to maintain an upright posture).  

            ---

            Question 5: (!!F)
            What deficits are characteristic of lesions to the spinocerebellum?

            Nystagmus, vertigo, and hearing loss.
            Spasticity, hyperreflexia, and positive Babinski sign.
            Truncal ataxia, limb ataxia
            Bradykinesia, resting tremor, and cogwheel rigidity.

            Correct Answer:  
            Truncal ataxia, limb ataxia (dysdiadochokinesia, dysmetria, action tremors), problems with balance and posture, inability to walk in tandem, and dysarthria.  

            Rationale:  
            The spinocerebellum (vermis and paravermal regions) is involved in regulating posture, equilibrium, and coordination of limb movements. Lesions to this area result in:  
            - Truncal ataxia (unsteadiness of the trunk),  
            - Limb ataxia, which includes:  
              - Dysdiadochokinesia (difficulty performing rapid alternating movements),  
              - Dysmetria (inability to accurately gauge movement distance), and  
              - Action tremors (tremors during voluntary movements).  
            - Problems with balance and posture,  
            - Inability to walk in tandem (heel-to-toe walking), and  
            - Dysarthria (slurred speech).  

            ---

            Question 6: (!!F)
            What specific deficits are associated with lesions to the cerebrocerebellum? 

            a.Nystagmus, vertigo, and hearing loss.
            b.Problems with coordination of fine finger.
            c.Spasticity, hypertonia, and clonus.
            d.Bradykinesia, rigidity, and postural instability.

            Correct Answer:  
            b.Problems with coordination of fine finger movements, dysarthria, and dysmetria.  

            Rationale:  
            The cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres) is involved in motor planning, initiation, and timing, as well as refining skilled movements. Lesions to this area result in:  
            - Difficulty coordinating fine finger movements,  
            - Dysarthria (slurred speech), and  
            - Dysmetria (inability to accurately gauge movement distance or force).

        .Motor Control
            Question 1:  
            According to McClure et al., what is the definition of motor control? 

            a) The ability to maintain balance and stability without voluntary movement
            b) The process of involuntary reflexive movements in response to sensory input
            c) The ability to plan, execute, and adapt goal-directed movements such that they are accurate, coordinated, and efficient
            d) The neural process of producing force in response to external stimuli 

            Correct Answer:  
            The ability to plan, execute, and adapt goal-directed movements such that they are accurate, coordinated, and efficient.  

            Rationale:  
            Motor control is defined as the ability to plan, execute, and adapt goal-directed movements in a way that ensures they are accurate, coordinated, and efficient. This definition emphasizes the importance of both the planning and execution phases of movement, as well as the ability to adapt movements based on feedback and changing conditions.  

            ---

            Question 2:  
            True or False: Motor control consists only of postural control.  

            Correct Answer: False  

            Rationale:  
            Motor control consists of two main components:  
                1. Postural control, which involves maintaining stability and balance.  
                2. Control of movement, which includes mobility (e.g., gait) and manipulation (e.g., reaching).  

            Thus, motor control is not limited to postural control but also encompasses the control of voluntary movements like walking and fine motor tasks such as reaching or grasping.

            Correct Answers:

            - Cognitive processing is not directly listed as a component of motor control in this context, although cognitive functions can influence motor planning and execution.
