All Objectives for Exam 1:
    ❖ General Principles
        ➢ Part 1
            ■ Explain the concept that behavior is a result of activation of functional neural circuitry and neuron to neuron communication.
                ● Behavior is the end product of a reaction (rxn) initiated by signaling in the brain. You cannot have the behavior without the signaling to do so, and you need to measure both to see efficacy of pathways.
                    Here's how I would explain the concept that behavior is the end product of signaling in the brain, in a way that a kid could understand:

                    Imagine your brain is like a big city, with lots of different buildings and roads. The buildings are like the nerve cells in your brain, and the roads are the connections between them. These nerve cells are constantly sending signals to each other, kind of like cars driving on the roads.

                    When you want to do something, like play a game or talk to a friend, your brain has to send a special set of signals through the roads to make it happen. These signals travel from one nerve cell to the next, until they reach the parts of your brain that control your muscles and voice.

                    Once the signals reach those parts, your muscles and voice start moving, and that's when you see the behavior - the actual playing of the game or talking to your friend. So the behavior you see is the end result of all the signaling that happened in your brain first.

                    You can't have the behavior without the brain signals to make it happen. It's like you can't drive a car without turning on the engine first. And to really understand how the brain works, scientists need to measure both the signals in the brain and the behaviors they produce, to see how the pathways in your brain are working.

            (Γ)Here's a mnemonic to help remember the different brain imaging techniques:
                PET: Positrons Emit Traces
                MRS: Metabolites Reveal Secrets
                fNIRS: Flowing Near-Infrared Signals
                EEG: Electrical Echoes Galore
                MEG: Magnetic Emanations Grasped
                fMRI: Flowing Blood Reveals Function

                To expand on the mnemonic:
                    PET: Positrons Emit Traces - PET uses positron-emitting radioactive tracers to measure brain activity.
                    MRS: Metabolites Reveal Secrets - MR Spectroscopy analyzes the chemical composition of brain tissue.
                    fNIRS: Flowing Near-Infrared Signals - fNIRS detects changes in blood oxygenation using near-infrared light.
                    EEG: Electrical Echoes Galore - EEG records the electrical activity of the brain.
                    MEG: Magnetic Emanations Grasped - MEG measures the magnetic fields generated by neural activity.
                    fMRI: Flowing Blood Reveals Function - fMRI maps brain activity by detecting changes in blood oxygenation.
                By associating each technique with a memorable phrase, you can more easily recall the key features and applications of these important neuroimaging methods.

            ■ Compare and contrast the methods for studying the nervous system
                ●  Structure infers function 
                    ◆ This is how you delineate Brodmann's areas.
                ● Imaging:
                    ◆ Physiological: PET, MR Spectroscopy, fNIRS - labels ions or tissues
                    ◆ Temporal: EEG, MEG - Magnetic measure superimposes image of activity
                    ◆ Functional: fMRI - tasked based working finds spatial brain areas working
                ● Best way to get a complete picture of what is going on is through multimodal imaging to combine temporal and spatial.
                    ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
                    PET (Positron Emission Tomography):
                        - Principle: PET measures brain activity by detecting positron-emitting radioactive tracers injected into the body.
                        - Advantages:
                            - Provides detailed images of brain function.
                            - Can detect changes at the molecular level.
                        - Limitations:
                            - Involves exposure to radiation.
                            - Limited temporal resolution.

                    MR Spectroscopy (MRS):
                        - Principle: MRS measures brain metabolites to assess brain function and biochemistry.
                        - Advantages:
                            - Non-invasive method to study brain chemistry.
                            - Can detect changes in neurotransmitters and metabolites.
                        - Limitations:
                            - Lower spatial resolution compared to other imaging techniques.

                    fNIRS (Functional Near-Infrared Spectroscopy):
                        - Principle: fNIRS measures changes in blood oxygen levels in the brain using near-infrared light.
                        - Advantages:
                            - Portable and less restrictive than other methods.
                            - Suitable for studying brain activity during natural movements.
                        - Limitations:
                            - Limited depth penetration compared to other imaging techniques.

                    EEG (Electroencephalography):
                        - Principle: EEG records electrical activity in the brain using electrodes placed on the scalp.
                        - Advantages:
                            - High temporal resolution, capturing rapid brain activity.
                            - Useful for studying sleep patterns and epilepsy.
                        - Limitations:
                            - Limited spatial resolution compared to imaging techniques like fMRI.

                    MEG (Magnetoencephalography):
                        - Principle: MEG measures magnetic fields produced by neuronal activity in the brain.
                        - Advantages:
                            - Directly measures neuronal activity with high temporal resolution.
                            - Provides precise timing information of brain processes.
                        - Limitations:
                            - Expensive and less available than EEG.

                    fMRI (Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging):
                        - Principle: fMRI detects changes in blood flow related to neural activity using magnetic fields and radio waves.
                        - Advantages:
                            - Excellent spatial resolution, mapping brain regions involved in tasks.
                            - Widely used for cognitive and clinical research.
                        - Limitations:
                            - Expensive and requires participants to lie still during scanning.

                    In summary, each brain imaging technique offers unique strengths and limitations, making them suitable for different research questions and applications. PET and fMRI provide detailed spatial information, while EEG and MEG offer exceptional temporal resolution. MR Spectroscopy and fNIRS focus on biochemical and oxygenation changes, respectively. Researchers choose these techniques based on the specific aspects of brain function they aim to investigate.

        ➢ Part 2
              ■ Define projection and association neurons/fibers, and interneurons
                 ● Projection: Ascending and descending pathways out to receptor, center, or target
                 ● Association: Integrate information within brain through superior longitudinal, uncinate, and inferior longitudinal fasciculi
                 ● Interneurons: Connect neuron to neuron. Allow for short distance talk
                    ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                    The given information provides definitions for three types of neurons/fibers in the nervous system:

                    Projection Neurons/Fibers

                    Projection neurons or fibers form ascending and descending pathways that connect different parts of the nervous system. They transmit information:
                    - From receptors to processing centers
                    - Between processing centers
                    - From processing centers to target organs or tissues

                    These neurons allow for long-distance communication within the nervous system, enabling sensory input to reach the brain and motor commands to reach muscles and glands.

                    Association Neurons/Fibers

                    Association neurons or fibers integrate information within the brain. They connect different regions of the cerebral cortex through specific pathways:
                    - Superior longitudinal fasciculus
                    - Uncinate fasciculus
                    - Inferior longitudinal fasciculus

                    These fibers facilitate higher-order processing and coordination between different functional areas of the brain, supporting complex cognitive functions.

                    Interneurons

                    Interneurons are local circuit neurons that:
                    - Connect one neuron to another
                    - Allow for short-distance communication within neural networks

                    They play a crucial role in processing and modulating information within specific regions of the nervous system, forming the basis for local neural circuits and information processing.

              ■ Describe the ordered communication between neurons
                 ● Neurons in groups take information through ganglia, nuclei, and cell columns to information centers
                 ● Serial vs Parallel Processing
                    ◆ Serial: “Chain-link” - a single disturbance can damage the signaling pathway.
                    ◆ Parallel: More than one path from point “A” to “B”
                        ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                        The ordered communication between neurons involves complex pathways and processing methods. Let's break down the key aspects:

                        Neuronal Information Flow

                        Neurons work in groups to transmit information through various structures:

                        1. Ganglia: Clusters of neuron cell bodies outside the central nervous system.
                        2. Nuclei: Groups of neuron cell bodies within the central nervous system.
                        3. Cell columns: Vertical arrangements of neurons in the brain or spinal cord.

                        These structures relay information to higher processing centers in the brain, allowing for integration and interpretation of signals.

                        Processing Methods

                        Neuronal communication employs two main processing strategies:

                        Serial Processing

                        - Characterized by a "chain-link" structure
                        - Information flows sequentially from one neuron to the next
                        - Vulnerable to disruption, as damage to a single point can break the entire signaling pathway

                        Parallel Processing

                        - Involves multiple pathways between two points ("A" to "B")
                        - Offers redundancy and increased reliability
                        - More resilient to localized damage or disruption

                        Parallel processing allows the nervous system to maintain function even if one pathway is compromised, providing a more robust communication network.

                        The combination of these processing methods and the organized structures of neuronal groups enables efficient and reliable information transmission throughout the nervous system.

              ■ Explain what is meant by the terms 'distributed control'.
                 ● AKA heterarchical control, horizontal control
                 ● It means responsibility for different motor actions are distributed among different regions of the CNS, and not all signals will be processed in the same way and go up the same “hierarchical” chain.
                    ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                    Distributed control, also known as heterarchical control or horizontal control, refers to a system of neural organization in the central nervous system (CNS) where:

                    1. Responsibility for different motor actions is spread across various regions of the CNS.
                    2. Neural signals are not processed uniformly or through a single hierarchical pathway.

                    This model of control implies that:

                    - Multiple brain areas can independently initiate and control motor actions.
                    - There is no strict top-down hierarchy in motor control.
                    - Different motor tasks may engage distinct neural networks.
                    - Parallel processing occurs, allowing for more flexible and efficient motor responses.

                    Distributed control contrasts with a purely hierarchical model, where all motor commands would flow through a single, linear chain of command. Instead, it allows for more complex and adaptable motor behaviors by utilizing the specialized capabilities of different brain regions simultaneously.

              ■ Explain how the organization of feedback enables distributed control.
                 ● Because all levels of the nervous system are in constant communication, it can manage heterarchical control. The feedback adds to the ‘talk’
                    ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                    The organization of feedback in the nervous system plays a crucial role in enabling distributed control, also known as heterarchical or horizontal control. This system of neural organization allows for more flexible and efficient motor responses by utilizing multiple brain areas simultaneously. Here's how feedback contributes to distributed control:

                    Constant Communication

                    All levels of the nervous system are in constant communication, creating a dynamic network of information exchange. This ongoing "talk" between different neural structures allows for:

                    1. Real-time adjustments to motor commands
                    2. Integration of sensory information from various sources
                    3. Coordination between different brain regions

                    Feedback Enhancement

                    The feedback loops within the nervous system enhance the distributed control by:

                    1. Providing continuous updates on the state of the body and environment
                    2. Allowing for rapid corrections and modifications to motor plans
                    3. Enabling parallel processing of information across multiple neural pathways

                    Adaptive Control

                    The feedback-driven distributed control system allows for:

                    1. More flexible responses to changing environmental conditions
                    2. Improved ability to handle complex motor tasks
                    3. Greater resilience to localized damage or disruption in the nervous system

                    By incorporating feedback at multiple levels, the nervous system can maintain efficient control without relying on a strict hierarchical structure, thus enabling the distributed, heterarchical control that characterizes many of our motor behaviors.

        ➢ Part 3
           ■ Explain how pre-wiring can enhance neural messaging
              ● Development is ordered and predictable for a species
                 ◆ Genetic determinants handle this
              ● 2 Methods
                 ◆ Divergence (diffuse influence)
                    ➢ Ascending pain information, Motor axon to muscle fibers
                 ◆ Convergent Integration
                    ➢ Association cortexes, Combined peripheral & descending inputs
                ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                Pre-wiring enhances neural messaging through genetically determined developmental processes that create organized and predictable neural structures. This pre-wiring occurs through two main methods:

                Divergence (Diffuse Influence)

                Divergence allows a single neuron to influence multiple targets:

                - Ascending pain information: Pain signals from a single source can spread to activate various brain regions, enabling a comprehensive pain response.
                - Motor axon to muscle fibers: One motor neuron can innervate multiple muscle fibers, allowing for coordinated muscle contractions.

                This pre-wired divergence enables efficient signal amplification and widespread influence from a single source.

                Convergent Integration

                Convergent integration combines inputs from multiple sources:

                - Association cortexes: These brain areas integrate information from various sensory modalities, allowing for complex cognitive processing.
                - Combined peripheral & descending inputs: Spinal cord neurons receive both sensory input from the periphery and motor commands from higher brain centers, enabling refined motor control.

                This pre-wired convergence facilitates complex information processing and integration of multiple neural signals.

                By establishing these pre-wired patterns during development, the nervous system can efficiently process and transmit information without having to create new connections for every neural interaction.

           ■ Explain how pre-wiring can reduce the degrees of freedom
              ● Removing DOF = removing variables that can impact signaling efficiency
              ● Feedforward & Feedback Inhibition
                 ◆ FF (reciprocal inhibition)
                    ➢ Helps when antagonist needs to be inhibited to allow agonist to function
                 ◆ FB (recurrent inhibition)
                    ➢ Helps with allowing for flexibility in future motions and rest in the agonist to avoid fatigue
                ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                Pre-wiring in the nervous system can effectively reduce the degrees of freedom (DOF) in neural signaling, thereby enhancing efficiency and control. This reduction in DOF is achieved through two main mechanisms:

                Removing Variables

                By pre-wiring certain neural pathways, the nervous system eliminates variables that could potentially impact signaling efficiency. This results in:

                1. More predictable neural responses
                2. Faster signal transmission
                3. Reduced computational load on the nervous system

                Feedforward and Feedback Inhibition

                Pre-wiring establishes specific inhibitory circuits that further reduce DOF:

                Feedforward Inhibition (Reciprocal Inhibition)

                - Helps when an antagonist muscle needs to be inhibited to allow the agonist to function effectively
                - Enhances movement precision by preventing unnecessary co-contraction
                - Reduces the number of possible muscle activation patterns, simplifying motor control

                Feedback Inhibition (Recurrent Inhibition)

                - Allows for flexibility in future motions
                - Provides a mechanism for the agonist muscle to rest, avoiding fatigue
                - Modulates neural activity, preventing over-excitation and promoting stability in neural circuits

                By incorporating these pre-wired inhibitory mechanisms, the nervous system can achieve more efficient and coordinated motor control with fewer variables to manage, effectively reducing the degrees of freedom in neural signaling and motor output.

    ❖ NS Development
          ➢ Part 1
              ■ Define the terms differentiation, neural patterning, gastrulation, and induction.
                  ● Differentiation - the diversification of neuronal stem cells into thousands of anatomically and functionally different types of neurons.  This is where neural circuits are formed 
                  ● Neural Patterning - Process by which NS cells acquire identities according to their specific spatial positions
                  ● Gastrulation - major developmental event where three germ layers are formed (fundamental aspects of the body plan are established)
                      ◆ Neurulation is the process of differentiation neural elements (neural plate, neural tube, neural crest)
                  ● Induction - determines rostral and caudal differentiation of neural tube
                    ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                    The given information defines four important terms related to neural development:

                    Differentiation

                    Differentiation is the process by which neuronal stem cells diversify into thousands of anatomically and functionally distinct types of neurons. This is a crucial stage in neural development as it is where neural circuits are formed, allowing for the complex functionality of the nervous system.

                    Neural Patterning

                    Neural patterning is the process through which nervous system cells acquire specific identities based on their spatial positions. This spatial organization is essential for the proper development and functioning of the nervous system.

                    Gastrulation

                    Gastrulation is a major developmental event during which the three germ layers are formed, establishing the fundamental aspects of the body plan. As part of this process, neurulation occurs, which involves the differentiation of neural elements, including:

                    - Neural plate
                    - Neural tube
                    - Neural crest

                    Induction

                    Induction is a developmental process that determines the rostral (head-end) and caudal (tail-end) differentiation of the neural tube. This process is crucial for establishing the basic organization of the central nervous system along its longitudinal axis.

                    These developmental processes work together to create the complex structure and function of the nervous system.

              ■ Compare and contrast endoderm, ectoderm and mesoderm cell layers in terms of their location in the embryo and what structures develop from them.
                  ● Endoderm - gives rise to organs/ viscera
                  ● Ectoderm - becomes the outer lining of the body and hair
                  ● Mesoderm - becomes muscle/ connective tissue. Gets added later and forms the notochord in midline. This induces the ectoderm to make a nervous system
                  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                  The endoderm, ectoderm, and mesoderm are the three primary germ layers that form during embryonic development. Here's a comparison of these layers:

                  Location in the Embryo

                  - Endoderm: Innermost layer
                  - Ectoderm: Outermost layer
                  - Mesoderm: Middle layer, added later in development

                  Structures Developed

                  Endoderm
                  - Gives rise to organs and viscera
                  - Develops into:
                    - Digestive tract lining
                    - Respiratory tract lining
                    - Liver
                    - Pancreas
                    - Thyroid gland

                  Ectoderm
                  - Becomes the outer lining of the body and hair
                  - Develops into:
                    - Skin and its appendages (hair, nails)
                    - Nervous system (induced by the mesoderm)
                    - Sensory organs (eyes, ears, nose)
                    - Tooth enamel

                  Mesoderm
                  - Becomes muscle and connective tissue
                  - Forms the notochord in the midline
                  - Develops into:
                    - Skeletal muscle
                    - Smooth muscle
                    - Cardiac muscle
                    - Bones
                    - Blood vessels
                    - Kidneys
                    - Gonads

                  Key Differences

                  1. Timing: Mesoderm is added later in development compared to endoderm and ectoderm.

                  2. Inductive role: The mesoderm, specifically the notochord, induces the ectoderm to form the nervous system.

                  3. Tissue types: Each layer gives rise to distinct tissue types, with the mesoderm forming a wider variety of tissues compared to the other two layers.

                  The formation and differentiation of these germ layers are crucial steps in embryonic development, leading to the complex organization of tissues and organs in the mature organism.

              ■ Describe the developmental event of gastrulation
                  ● Once the ecto, endo, and mesoderm are formed, gastrulation has occurred and neurulation begins.
                  ● Notochord creates neural plate (neural tube/CNS) and neural crest (PNS)
                  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                  Gastrulation is a critical developmental event in embryogenesis that establishes the three primary germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. This process sets the foundation for the formation of various tissues and organs in the developing organism. Here’s a detailed description of gastrulation:

                  Key Aspects of Gastrulation

                  1. Formation of Germ Layers:
                     - Gastrulation leads to the differentiation of the embryo into three distinct layers:
                       - Endoderm: The innermost layer that will give rise to internal organs such as the digestive tract, liver, and lungs.
                       - Mesoderm: The middle layer that develops into muscles, bones, and connective tissues, as well as the circulatory system.
                       - Ectoderm: The outermost layer that forms the skin and nervous system.

                  2. Neurulation:
                     - Once gastrulation is complete and the germ layers are established, neurulation begins. This is the process by which the ectoderm differentiates to form the neural plate, which subsequently folds to create the neural tube.
                     - The notochord, a rod-like structure derived from mesoderm, plays a crucial role in this process by signaling the ectoderm to form the neural plate.

                  3. Development of Neural Structures:
                     - The neural plate eventually develops into:
                       - Neural Tube: This structure becomes the central nervous system (CNS), including the brain and spinal cord.
                       - Neural Crest: Cells that migrate from the edges of the neural plate and contribute to the peripheral nervous system (PNS) and other structures such as facial cartilage and pigment cells.

                  Importance of Gastrulation

                  Gastrulation is fundamental for establishing body plan organization and ensuring that cells are positioned correctly to develop into specific tissues and organs. It is a highly orchestrated process involving cell movements, shape changes, and signaling pathways that dictate cell fate.

                  In summary, gastrulation is a pivotal event in embryonic development that lays down the essential groundwork for forming complex structures in multicellular organisms. Its successful execution is vital for normal development and proper functioning of the organism.

              ■ Describe the 3-vesicle and 5-vesicle stages of brain formation
                  ● 3 vesicle - Forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain
                      ◆ 2 flexures (cephalic, cervical)
                  ● 5 vesicle - Telencephalon & Diencephalon (forebrain), Mesencephalon (midbrain), Metencephalon & Myelencephalon (hindbrain)
                      ◆ 3 flexures
                          ➢ Cephalic flexure (only one that remains in adulthood), pontine & cervical flexures
                    ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                    The 3-vesicle stage and 5-vesicle stage of brain formation represent key stages in the development of the embryonic brain, where the neural tube differentiates into distinct regions that will form the central nervous system. Below is a detailed comparison of these stages:

                    3-Vesicle Stage
                    - This is an early stage of brain development.
                    - The neural tube differentiates into three primary vesicles:
                      1. Forebrain (Prosencephalon): The most rostral (front) vesicle.
                      2. Midbrain (Mesencephalon): The middle vesicle.
                      3. Hindbrain (Rhombencephalon): The most caudal (rear) vesicle.

                    - Flexures:
                      - Two flexures (bends) form during this stage:
                        - Cephalic Flexure: Found between the forebrain and midbrain.
                        - Cervical Flexure: Found between the hindbrain and spinal cord.

                    5-Vesicle Stage
                    - This is a later stage of brain development where the primary vesicles further subdivide into five secondary vesicles:
                      1. Telencephalon (from the forebrain): Forms the cerebral hemispheres.
                      2. Diencephalon (from the forebrain): Forms structures like the thalamus, hypothalamus, and retina.
                      3. Mesencephalon (remains as the midbrain): Forms structures like the tectum and tegmentum.
                      4. Metencephalon (from the hindbrain): Forms the pons and cerebellum.
                      5. Myelencephalon (from the hindbrain): Forms the medulla oblongata.

                    - Flexures:
                      - Three flexures are present:
                        - Cephalic Flexure: Persists into adulthood and is responsible for the bend in the human brain's axis.
                        - Pontine Flexure: Located in the hindbrain; contributes to separating the metencephalon from the myelencephalon.
                        - Cervical Flexure: Separates the hindbrain from the spinal cord.

                    Summary of Key Differences

                    | Characteristic          | 3-Vesicle Stage            | 5-Vesicle Stage                                                       |
                    |-----------------------------|--------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
                    | Number of Vesicles          | 3                              | 5                                                                         |
                    | Vesicles Present            | Forebrain, Midbrain, Hindbrain | Telencephalon, Diencephalon, Mesencephalon, Metencephalon, Myelencephalon |
                    | Flexures                    | Cephalic, Cervical             | Cephalic, Pontine, Cervical                                               |
                    | Developmental Complexity    | Early differentiation          | Advanced differentiation with specific brain regions forming              |

                    These stages are critical for organizing the structure and function of the central nervous system, with each vesicle contributing to specific adult brain structures.

              ■ Explain the relationship of ventricles to regions of the brain
                  ● Lateral ventricles - Telencephalon (cerebral hemispheres, basal ganglia
                  ● Third ventricle - Diencephalon (Thalamus and hypothalamus)
                  ● CA - Mesencephalon
                  ● 4th ventricle - Metencephalon (pons and cerebellum) & myelencephalon (medulla oblongata)
                  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------
                  The relationship of the brain's ventricles to the regions of the brain is crucial for understanding the organization and function of the central nervous system. Here’s a detailed explanation of how each ventricle corresponds to specific brain regions:

                  Ventricles and Their Associated Brain Regions

                  1. Lateral Ventricles
                  - Location: Found within the telencephalon, which comprises the cerebral hemispheres.
                  - Structures Developed: The lateral ventricles are associated with the development of:
                    - Cerebral hemispheres
                    - Basal ganglia
                  - Function: They are responsible for the production and circulation of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which provides cushioning, nutrient transport, and waste removal.

                  2. Third Ventricle
                  - Location: Located in the diencephalon, situated between the two halves of the thalamus.
                  - Structures Developed: The third ventricle is linked to:
                    - Thalamus
                    - Hypothalamus
                  - Function: It also contains CSF and plays a role in regulating various autonomic functions through its connection to surrounding structures.

                  3. Cerebral Aqueduct (CA)
                  - Location: This narrow channel runs through the mesencephalon (midbrain).
                  - Function: The cerebral aqueduct connects the third ventricle to the fourth ventricle, allowing for the flow of CSF between these cavities.

                  4. Fourth Ventricle
                  - Location: Positioned in both the metencephalon (which includes the pons and cerebellum) and the myelencephalon (which includes the medulla oblongata).
                  - Structures Developed: The fourth ventricle is associated with:
                    - Pons
                    - Cerebellum
                    - Medulla oblongata
                  - Function: It serves as a conduit for CSF to flow into the central canal of the spinal cord and also allows CSF to exit into the subarachnoid space surrounding the brain and spinal cord.

                  Summary of Relationships

                  | Ventricle          | Associated Brain Region | Structures Developed                           |
                  |------------------------|-----------------------------|----------------------------------------|
                  | Lateral Ventricles     | Telencephalon               | Cerebral hemispheres, basal ganglia    |
                  | Third Ventricle        | Diencephalon                | Thalamus, hypothalamus                 |
                  | Cerebral Aqueduct      | Mesencephalon               | Connects third and fourth ventricles   |
                  | Fourth Ventricle       | Metencephalon & Myelencephalon | Pons, cerebellum, medulla oblongata |

                  Understanding this relationship helps clarify how different parts of the brain communicate and function together, as well as how cerebrospinal fluid circulates through these critical structures.

    ❖ Neuron Communication
                ➢ 1C (potentials)
                ■ Define the resting membrane potential (RMP) of a neuron
                ● RMP is an electrical gradient that is maintained by a separation of
                charges across the membrane. The selectively permeable


                membrane allows certain ions to pass through, primarily through
                sodium/potassium pumps.
                ● Neuron: -70mV inside, Muscle: -90mV inside
                ■ Define the terms depolarization and hyperpolarization
                ● Hyperpolarization is an increase in RMP. It causes inhibition -
                makes it less likely that an AP will fire.
                ● Depolarization is a decrease in RMP. It causes excitation, and
                makes it more likely to send an AP.
                ■ Describe the 2 types of local potentials
                ● Local potentials
                ◆ Receptor potentials (RP)
                ➢ Generated at peripheral receptor of a sensory
                neuron
                ◆ Synaptic potentials (SP)
                ➢ Generated at a postsynaptic membrane
                ● Action potentials
                ◆ Depolarizing signal that is propagated down the axon
                ■ Compare/contrast local potentials versus action potentials
                ● Local potentials can be positive or negative, and decay over space
                and time. They will sum both spatially and temporally in an effort
                to bring the RMP to threshold. If the RMP hits threshold near the
                trigger zone (axon hillock), then an AP will be fired. An AP does
                not degrade as it is propagated down the axon.
                ■ Describe action potential propagation and the factors that relate to
                speed of conduction.
                ● Propagation of an AP is the process by which the action potential
                will “jump” down the axon from node of ranvier to node of ranvier.
                These nodes are areas that are in between myelin sheaths that
                have great density of Na/K pumps and therefore extreme electrical
                activity.
                ● The greater the diameter of the axon or more myelin present, the
                faster the signal is conducted.
                ➢ 2a (actions at synapse) pt. 1
                ■ Describe the sequence of events leading to release of
                neurotransmitter by the presynaptic neuron
                ● Influx of Ca++ promotes synaptic vesicle fusion with presynaptic
                membrane, which will release the NTs into the synapse. This
                happens when an AP reaches the end of the axon terminal and
                changes the voltage.
                ■ Describe the sequence of events during synaptic transmission from
                a pre- to postsynaptic neuron
                ● NT released into synaptic cleft response to AP in presynaptic cell
                ● NT diffuses and binds to postsynaptic receptor


                ● Ion channel chemically activated, ions move, synaptic potential
                generated
                ● Synaptic potential passive spread to trigger zone, if sufficient
                generates AP or inhibits AP response
                ■ Describe the differences in characteristics between excitatory vs
                inhibitory central synapses
                ● Excitatory: Asymmetric - gray type 1
                ● Inhibitory: Symmetric - gray type 2
                ■ Compare and contrast axodendritic, axosomatic and axoaxonic
                synapses.
                ● Axodendritic - can be excitatory or inhibitory
                ● Axosomatic - usually inhibitory
                ● Axoaxonic - always inhibitory
                ● Bc of location of axodendritic and axosomatic, axosomatic has a
                greater influence on the triggering of an AP. The axodendritic local
                potentials degrade more by the time they reach the trigger zone.n

                ● The result of intrinsic and extrinsic processes. Frequency of AP or
                steady state changes to influx of ions can both cause changes in
                efficacy at the synapse. Plasticity is the way in which the synapse
                will adapt to the demands the neurons put on it.
                ■ Describe intrinsic and extrinsic processes of synaptic plasticity
                ● Intrinsic

                by its own activity
                ● Extrinsic
                ◆ Extrinsic processes can come in the forms of steady state
                changes to influx of Ca++ or frequency of AP stimulation.
                Both of these extrinsic signals cause intrinsic changes to

                ■ Describe the pathology in Myasthenia Gravis and Lamberton-Eaton
                Myasthenic Syndrome
                ● Both are issues with Acetylcholinesterase deficiencies. Impairing
                the way Ach functions on a muscle impairs use of motor system.
                ● MG:
                ◆ POSTsynaptic dysfunction
                ◆ Causes an abnormal amount of repetitive responses,
                quickly fatiguing muscles


                ● Myasthenic Syndrome:
                ◆ PREsynaptic dysfunction
                ◆ Difficulty initiating adequate muscle contraction

    ❖ Neuroplasticity
                ➢ Part 1
                ■ Define experience dependent plasticity and critical periods
                ● At birth there is a ‘rough draft’ of neural circuits that are genetically
                determined. After this, the neural circuitry is refined by experience
                in a process called experience- dependent reorganization.
                ● Critical periods are periods in which the nervous system’s
                sensitivity to modifications is heightened.
                ■ Describe examples of experience dependent plasticity and critical
                periods during development
                ● Experience - Longitudinal studies of orphans raised in institutions
                vs. with families.
                ◆ In an fMRI there are notable structural changes in frontal
                lobes. This development is delayed and is especially
                noticeable in the uncinate fasciculus
                ➢ Uncinate fasciculus is a long range white matter
                tract that connects limbic regions to the temporal
                and frontal lobes. It develops into the 30s, and
                atypical development is seen in social deprivation,
                autism spectrum disorders, and substance abuse.
                ◆ Somatotopic organization for people with syndactyly is
                another example.
                ● Critical periods -
                ◆ Monocular deprivation in baby monkeys
                ➢ Changes to representation of eye fields on visual
                cortex was altered dramatically even though there
                was no injury because of a lack of external
                stimulus. This deprivation altered the cortical
                structure.
                ➢ Part 2
                ■ Describe the evidence of cortical reorganization in animals and
                humans after training and injury/disease.
                ● Syndactyly
                ◆ Cortical remapping by use occurs post corrective surgery,
                allowing for a new cortical remapping to occur
                ● Phantom limb
                ◆ Amputees can gain expanded areas of cortex in their
                homunculi from nearby areas into the area of the lost
                extremity (ex: pursed lip breathing tasks can show that the
                face lights up areas that used to be occupied by an
                amputated upper limb)


                ➢ Part 3
                ■ Describe the changes in synapses/long term potentiation underlying
                neuroplasticity
                ● LTP - Long lasting increase in the amplitude of the excitatory
                postsynaptic potentials (glutamate - AMPA and NMDA receptors)
                ◆ Silent - lack functional glutamate AMPA receptors
                ◆ 1.) Normal synaptic transmission occurs
                ◆ 2.) Retrograde messenger from post synaptic dendrite
                goes back to pre synaptic cell to initiate LTP
                ◆ 3.) Additional AMPA receptors will deposit along the post
                synaptic neuron so lesser signals from the presynaptic
                neuron needs less stimulus to get a greater signal across
                the synapse.
                ◆ This process - over time - will take a mobile synapse that is
                likely to be pruned and, if it is used enough, turn it into a
                permanent mushroom spine. Mushrooms are MUCH more
                efficient for signaling due to the additional action at the
                synapse.
                ■ Describe neuroplasticity related to recovery from injury
                ● After a stroke/ traumatic injury
                ◆ Directly: If neurons are deprived of oxygen for a longer
                time they will die/ will not regenerate
                ◆ Indirectly: Oxygen-deprived neurons will release a large
                amount of glutamate. This glutamate is excitatory, which
                will in turn cause a massive influx of calcium and cause
                excitotoxicity.
                ● Mechanisms to overcome some of the damage
                ◆ Synaptic effectiveness
                ➢ Following cortical injury, edema compresses
                neuron and causes a local ischemia. When the
                edema resolves the issue resolves.
                ◆ Denervation hypersensitivity
                ➢ Additional receptor sites will appear on post
                synaptic neuron to make it receptive to undamaged
                neurons
                ◆ Synaptic hyper effectiveness
                ➢ After loss of synapses, remaining branches will
                release greater amounts of NTs than it would’ve
                normally.
                ◆ Unmasking of silent synapses
                ➢ Normally unused synapses become activated

    Vision
                ● Part 1
                ○ Describe the primary visual pathway for seeing
                ■ Retina - Optic nerve - Optic Chiasm - Optic tract - Lateral geniculate
                nucleus (LGN) - Optic radiations (through parietal and temporal cortex) -
                Visual cortex
                ○ Describe how visual information is integrated and combined to form a
                representation of an object
                ■ Photoreceptors
                ● Cones - Acuity and color
                ○ Highest concentration is at fovea, which is where lens tries
                to keep the highest concentration of light
                ● Rods - color-blind; better for motion
                ● These two in addition to amacrine, horizontal cells, bipolar, etc.
                take in a lot of information before leaving the retina.
                ■ Integration
                ● Magnocellular
                ○ “M” Cells
                ○ Where and how?
                ● Ventral - parvocellular
                ○ “P” Cells
                ○ What?
                ■ Relates information you have to what it is
                ● Example from GMOMM:
                “You are thinking about the meeting that you really do not want to attend as you are about to cross the street.
                Suddenly, out of the corner of your eye there is a flash, a large object moving towards you. You jump back! It is only
                after you are back safely on the curb that the full perspective of the incident hits you. Now you recognize a person
                with a portable phone to his ear driving through the intersection (and the red light) in his red sports car. After catching
                your breath, you have the appropriate response to the situation. The moral of the story? Remember what you have
                been taught: pay attention, look both ways before crossing. Now are you not glad that you have a fast, preconscious
                Magno visual pathway for quick action and a conscious (slower, Parvo) pathway for high level perception (make of
                car & license ); and of course a limbic system to react in an 'appropriate' manner.“
                Fig 12-37. Magnocellular and Parvocellular Visual Pathways: In A Flash Movie (gec). GO TO:gmornm.pitt.edu 25
                GMOMMBook PPA32481 Pathway
                ○ Compare and contrast the dorsal and ventral visual streams
                ■ Dorsal stream for action
                ● Goes to lateral premotor regions
                ● Visually guided reaching
                ○ PMd (premotor dorsal) via medial dorsal and medial intra
                parietal areas
                ○ Translates visual info about object location to reaching
                direction
                ● Visually informed grasping
                ○ Translates visual information about object poperties into
                successful grasping (feedforward)
                ○ PMv (premotor ventral) via anterior intraparietal areas


                ■ Ventral stream for object recognition
                ● Convergent information
                ● Inferior temporal cortex codes complex integrated information
                ● Highly networked region has connections to prefrontal cortex
                ○ Has to do with recognition and experience
                ○ Describe how we use vision for feedback and feedforward control.
                ■ FF
                ● Allows for you to prepare for an event prior to its occurrence
                ■ FB
                ● Command specifies desired state rather than a response.
                ■ Ball example:
                ● FF: Activate muscle prior to displacement as an anticipatory
                response
                ● FB: If eyes were closed, there’s a significant response to
                occurrence but no anticipatory
                ● Part 2
                ○ Describe the function and pathways involved for triggered and attention
                saccades.
                ■ Saccades voluntary or reflexive response (majority voluntary), shift the
                fovea rapidly to a new visual target
                ● Redirects the center of sight to scan environment quickly
                ● ~900 degrees per second
                ● Occurs several times/sec
                ● In between saccades there are fixations for 100-200ms
                ■ Triggered (reflexive)
                ● Something moves in visual field - detect
                ■ Attention (voluntary)
                ● Visual attention to something in the visual fiel
                ○ Input from frontal eye fields, posterior parietal cortex to
                superior colliculus to pontine brainstem centers for gaze
                control
                ○ Basal ganglia input to superior colliculus inhibits sup
                colliculus and suppress saccades
                ■ Ex: performing a well-learned motor skill, not
                interested in distraction of detect or find saccade
                eye movements
                ○ Describe the function and pathway involved for smooth pursuits
                ■ Smooth Pursuit: keeps the image of a moving target on the fovea
                ● Match eye speed to target speed
                ● Max of ~100 degrees per second
                ■ Information about object movement from the visual association cortex to
                middle temporal cortex to frontal eye fields projected to pontine nuclei and
                to the cerebellum and vestibular nuclei and onto pontine centers for gaze
                movement control


                ■ Cerebellum & vestibular system involved to integrate speed of movement
                of the object of interest into the smooth pursuit eye movement.
                ● Similar to motor copy integration in cerebellum
                ○ Describe how the size and distance of a target affects movement
                ■ Moving to a target, the size of the target influences the speed of
                movement
                ■ Your grasp posture adjusts as you approach to the size of the object to
                pick it up
                ■ The size of the image is a low-level visual process - represented in
                primary visual cortex and little extra processing involved
                ○ Describe how the familiarity of an object influences movement
                ■ Familiar size requires high-level visual processing; much integration
                including memory and recall.
                ● Occurs in parietal-temporal association cortex regions.
                ■ Reaching to a target, study the trajectory of the reach. Expect the
                movement to be continuous, smooth and generally at a constant velocity
                to target.
                ● Hesitancy, path deviations, speed inconsistency are features of
                disrupted trajectory
                ■ Reaching to target experiment: visually-guided, intended movement, ‘I
                want to reach to that object ...’
                ● A highly salient object distractor in the environment – a meaningful
                recognized [familiar] object has less impact on reach trajectory
                than less salient objects!! (Moher, Anderson & Song, 2015)
                ■ Summary: Recognition of an object means it take far less time to process
                as long as it is congruent with your preconceived beliefs.
                ● Part 3
                ○ Define tau and optical flow
                ■ Tau
                ● Time to contact
                ● Expansion of an object on the retina
                ● Very powerful predictive information, feedforward
                ■ Optic Flow
                ● Refers to the pattern of rays of light that strike the retina that
                emanate from and are specific to objects and features in the
                environment
                ● Visual information streaming past you
                ● Stoplight effect
                ○ Describe how tau influences movement
                ■ Savelsbergh study
                ● Nonconscious adaptation to size of ball without participants
                knowing it deflated
                ■ Long jump
                ● Step lengths of the last few steps vary across trials


                ○ Using visual information to specify time to contact of
                take-off board
                ○ Describe how optical flow influences balance
                ■ Moving room
                ● Floor is stationary, surroundings move. Adults sway back and forth
                in response to the flow, young children will often fall because they
                don’t have enough experience with optic flow yet.

    Vestibular and Auditory Systems
                ● Part 1
                ○ Describe basic anatomy of the vestibular apparatus
                ■ Fluid filled chambers in petrous portion of temporal bone: “Inner sock
                within an outer boot”
                ● Outer chamber
                ○ Osseous labyrinth filled with perilymph fluid
                ● Inner membranous labyrinth filled with endolymph
                ○ Vestibular apparatus
                ○ Cochlea
                ○ Explain how the vestibular apparatus detects and conveys motion and
                position of the head
                ■ Kinesthesis - sense of self motion
                ■ Vestibular system uses the motion of our head to detect kinesthesis. This
                information is used to stabilize eyes for vision, along with maintenance
                and recovery of balance.
                ● System receptors are specialized neurosensory hair cells:
                ○ Cilia extend from apical surface
                ■ Multiple stereocilia, one kinocilia
                ○ NT released from base of cell
                ○ Mechanism of activating the cell
                ■ Cilia deflect towards the cell depolarizes, while
                deflecting away hyperpolarizes.
                ■ Depolarization - increase release of NT,
                hyperpolarization - decreased release of NT
                ○ Efferents - filter and facilitate afferents
                ● Otolith organs
                ○ Membranous sacs within the vestibular apparatus
                ○ Utricle and Saccule detect
                ■ Static equilibrium (head relative to gravity)
                ■ Linear acceleration
                ● Horizontal - utricle; Vertical - saccule
                ■ Both use hair cells called macula to detect these
                alterations
                ● Orientation of kinocilia in gelatinous
                membrane topped by otoconia provides
                directional sensitivity


                ○ Explain the importance of functional pairing of semicircular canals to
                directional sensitivity
                ■ 3 canals per side, pair with opposite side to detect angular acceleration
                ● R horizontal with L horizontal
                ● R anterior vertical with L posterior vertical
                ● R posterior vertical with L anterior vertical
                ● The opposition allows for kinocilia in one ear saying “turning this
                way” and the other side to say “not turning towards this side”
                ○ This pairing causes a reciprocal signalling
                ■ All 3 canals are off of the utricle and saccule. They use hair cells on the
                ampulla that project cilia into the gelatinous mass known as the cupula
                ● Part 2
                ○ Describe how information from the semicircular canals is used for head,
                neck and eye movement control
                ■ Semicircular canals go to medial and superior vestibular nuclei, which
                output to MLF.
                ● Ascending MLF - eye movement
                ● Descending MLF - spinal cord for head/neck control
                ○ Describe how information from the otolith organs is used for head, neck
                and eye movement control
                ■ Otoliths send to
                ● (Via semicircular canals) lateral vestibulospinal tract
                ● descending nucleus, which in turn has output to cerebellum,
                reticular formation, and contralateral vestibular nuclei
                ○ Describe the central divergence of vestibular information
                ■ There’s no primary vestibular target
                ■ Information has thalamic and cortical targets
                ● Thalamic - ventral basal, posterior nuclei
                ● Cortical -
                ○ Parietal temporal junction: including posterior (periarcuate
                vestibular area, small circle) parietal association areas;
                ventral intraparietal (VIP) area; medial superior temporal
                (MST)(visual association); parieto-insular vestibular cortex
                (PIVC)
                ○ Primary somatosensory (3a); near frontal eye fields
                ○ Describe the three vestibulo-ocular reflexes
                ■ 3 reflexes:
                ● Rotational vestibulo-ocular: with head rotation, eyes move
                opposite head (slow phase); quick reset (fast phase)
                ● Translational vestibulo-ocular: with visual image, linear motion,
                close objects moving fast, far objects moving slower: otoliths
                stabilize eyes for far object
                ● Ocular counter-rolling response: with head tilt, otoliths stabilize
                eyes to correct for vertical offset


                ■ Vestibular nucleus neurons involved in keeping visual image stable on
                retina
                ● Position-vestibular pause (PVP): primary for reflex, receive regular
                afferent inputs and transmit information about head in passive
                head movement
                ● Floccular target (FTN): Modulate/calibrate the reflex. Receive
                irregular afferent inputs and inputs from flocculus

                ● Part 3
                ○ Describe the auditory transduction of sound from the outer, middle to inner
                ear.
                ■ Catch, transform, deflect
                ■ Catch sound waves - outer ear
                ● Tensor tympani muscle tightens tympanic membrane for loud
                sound protection
                ■ Transform waves to vibrations - Middle ear
                ● Stapedius muscle pulls stapes out of oval window for sound power
                protection
                ■ Deflect pressure waves - inner ear
                ● Neurosensory unit activated for sound reception/representation in
                afferent firing pattern
                ○ Describe the structure and function of the Organ of Corti
                ■ Located in cochlea in inner ear
                ● Outer chambers of cochlea are filled with perilymph
                ○ Scala vestibule/scala tympani
                ● Inner chamber filled with endolymph
                ○ Scala media/ location of organ of Corti
                ■ Neurosensory cells allow for hearing
                ● Have stereocilia embedded in tectorial membrane
                ● Vibrations of the basilar membrane creates back and forth motion
                of the stereocilia and a sinusoidal wave of depolarization and
                hyperpolarization at the frequency of the sound
                ○ Explain how the cochlea discriminates frequencies, loudness and rhythm
                ■ Frequency - Pitch (cycles/sec = hz)
                ● Basilar membrane mechanical resonance contributes to frequency
                encoding
                ○ Different parts of membrane are different levels of stiffness
                and therefore resonate at different frequencies
                ○ Stiff oval window - high pitch
                ○ Flexible near apex - Low pitch
                ■ Loudness - amplitude of sound wave
                ● Louder = broader range of basilar membrane vibration and greater
                number of discharges of the hair cells and afferent nerve
                ■ Rhythm
                ● Discharge duration of the hair cells


                ■ Hair cells have both mechanical and electrical resonance. The
                mechanical resonance amplifies the electrical resonance.

                ○ Describe the similarities and differences in central auditory pathways that
                serve to identify sounds versus locate sounds
                ■ Hear - dorsal cochlear nucleus —> (lateral lemniscus, inferior colliculus,
                MGN) —> Primary auditory cortex
                ● A lesion to (basically any aspect of) this chain will cause hearing
                issues in both ears
                ■ Localize sound
                ● Also uses inputs from both ears
                ● Ventral cochlear nucleus to sensory olivary nucleus bilaterally. The
                difference in timing and intensity received by SON is used to
                localize sound
                ○ Describe the primary auditory cortex, the different streams of cortical
                processing, and the connection to the motor system
                ■ Neurons in primary auditory cortex are arranged tonotopically
                ■ Auditory neurons are either excited by input from both ears or by one ear
                only
                ■ Ventral stream -> what is it
                ■ Dorsal -> where/how
                ■ Superior temporal gyrus has connections to inferior frontal gyrus and
                pre-SMA/SMA
                Somatosensation
                ● Pt 1
                ○ List six different sensory receptors and describe the modality that each
                responds to
                ■ Low threshold mechanoreceptors - discriminative touch (spatial and
                temporal acuity are high)
                ● RA, SA, PC
                ■ High threshold mechanoreceptors - pain
                ■ Thermal receptors - warm and cool
                ■ Proprioceptors - body and limb position, movement and force
                ■ Nociceptors - noxious mechanical, chemical, thermal
                ■ Polymodal receptors - discomfort, itch, hurt
                ○ Describe the four different types of low threshold mechanoreceptors and
                their role in active touch
                ■ RA1 - Meissner Corpuscle
                ● Clearly defined, small receptive field
                ● Most common in human body
                ■ RA2 - PC
                ● Large receptive field, less defined
                ● Respond to vibrations and detection of texture


                ■ SA1 - Merkel’s disk
                ● Clearly defined, small receptive field
                ● Sustained response - ex: holding a fragile object that you want to
                maintain a specific amount of pressure
                ■ SA2 - Ruffini ending
                ● Large receptive fields with directional preferences coded by
                groups of receptors. Less common in humans than other animals
                ○ Define receptive field and explain the importance of the receptive field to
                discriminative touch
                ■ Area of skin that results in a consistent response from the neuron when
                stimulated with the appropriate stimulus
                ■ Important for discriminative active touch
                ● A process by which humans actively seek tactile information
                ○ Describe the transduction of noxious stimuli to neural signals
                ■ Intense stimuli activate high threshold mechanoreceptors. Potential to
                damage/kill tissue is detected with pain, mechanical deformation, or
                chemicals
                ■ Pain afferents are small fibers (a delta and c fibers) which then project to
                neurons in the dorsal horn. Through HPC, TS, NS and WDR, the signal is
                projected up the spinothalamic tract on the opposite side of the spinal
                cord and ascends to the thalamus
                ○ Explain how the CNS can modulate pain
                ■ The CNS can modulate pain by using stimulus produced analgesia (SPA)
                and endogenous opiates
                ■ Neurons in the nucleus raphe magnus can provide serotonergic
                descending projections to the opiate interneuron which will then
                presynaptically inhibit the pain pathways with axoaxonic synapses.
                ● Pt. 2
                ○ Define the terms kinesthesis and proprioception
                ■ The ability to sense the position and location and orientation and
                movement of the body and its parts
                ● Without vision
                ● Uses muscle proprioceptors, joint receptors, cutaneous
                receptors, vestibular system
                ●  - muscle sense of moving, tension, and effort. Happens through
                muscle spindles and GTO
                ■ Proprioception
                ● About position, motion, force, and effort
                ○ Describe the structure of the muscle spindle and explain its role in
                kinesthesia
                ■ Embedded in skeletal muscle (extrafusal muscle) and senses changes in
                muscle length/rate
                ■ Each spindle has:
                ● Intrafusal muscle fibers - contractile fibers within the spindle


                ○ Central non-contractile region
                ○ Polar ends that are contractile and attached to extrafusal
                ● Sensory - connected to the non contractile regions
                ● Motor - both ends contractile regions
                ○ Describe alpha-gamma coactivation
                ■ Simultaneous activation of alpha and gamma motor neurons in a
                voluntary, actively contracting muscle
                ■ Critical to keep the spindle sensitive and ready to sense stretch
                ■ If just alpha were active, muscle spindle would lose sensitivity in
                intrafusal muscle. Gamma activation causes this contraction of intrafusal
                muscle to keep the muscle spindle sensitive to the extrafusal muscle.
                ○ Describe the structure of the golgi tendon organ and its role in kinesthesia
                ■ GTO has greatest concentration at the musculotendinous junction. It is in
                series with the fibers (unlike parallel spindles). The afferent 1b fibers that
                control it are woven into the collagen fibers of the tendon, so a contraction
                elicits a response.
                ■ Controlled by 1b axons, which signal in series. The effect on the spinal
                cord is therefore disynaptic
                ■ Need both types of efferents bc they allow an incredibly specific
                sensitivity/modulation of sensitivities
                ■ Because of the location, they allow continuous indication on force of
                contraction and changes. Gives protective qualities to GTO.
                ○ Explain how the combined function of spindles and golgi tendon organs
                enhances kinesthesia
                ■ In voluntary motion, the muscle spindles (acting in series, with 1a
                afferents) will signal the notion of change in muscle length and velocity of
                change. The 1b afferents that are in the collagen at the musculotendinous
                junction will then be squeezed as the muscle contracts, signaling the GTO
                to enact its protective action in spreading workload and resisting fatigue.
                ● Pt. 3
                ○ Name and describe the two major ascending sensory systems to conscious
                perception
                ■ Both have 3 neuron chains, both have first order in the DRG, both have
                third order to the primary somatosensory cortex. Difference is second
                order neuron (where it crosses). Both carry touch sensation so you can
                NOT distinguish them with light touch.
                ■ DCML
                ● Transmits joint position, vibration, and discriminative touch
                ■ ST
                ● Transmits pain and temperature information
                ○ Name and describe the two pathways to unconscious perception
                ■ Both go to the cerebellum for nonconscious interpretation of information.
                Continuous supply of information from dorsal and ventral horns allows for
                continuous awareness of position in space.


                ■ VCST
                ● Motor copy
                ● Clinically cannot be tested for, but helps keep motions smooth to
                allow for feedFORWARD corrections. Don’t need to wait til you’ve
                made an error to change action.
                ■ DCST
                ● Large fiber afferents that help with perception of movement,
                position, and effort. Muscle spindles and GTOs give a large
                amount of the information to this tract.
                ○ Describe the somatosensory homunculus
                ■ Topographical map on the postcentral gyrus that shows somatotopic
                distribution of body on the brain. Laterally is head/upper extremity, as you
                go medial you hit hips then legs drop over medial portion of the brain.
                ○ Explain the importance of inhibition to sensory perception; define the
                terms surround inhibition and motor gating
                ■ “Mexican Hat”
                ● If you were to not use surround inhibition, you could not pinpoint a
                stimulus. Any and all sensors in the region of the skin affected
                would fire the same and a “blob” of information would come in the
                response.
                ● Stimuli that are not as strong as the surrounding ones get
                inhibited, meaning only the very specific, strongest stimuli can
                pass through. This means you can target more exact locations of
                signals.
                ○ Define interoception and describe the role of cortical areas in
                self-awareness.
                ■ Interoception is an awareness of self. It’s how we know how we feel at
                any point in the sense of bladder, hunger, integration of sensory
                environment, motivation, behavior, thinking, etc.
                ■ A product of many areas of the brain, but primarily the insular cortex and
                anterior portions of the cingulate gyrus.

                 -Dura mater - meningeal layer(''): tough layer, inferior to periosteal layer, side borders of Superior sagittal sinus('')
                 -Subarachnoid space('Meninges.jpg'): deep to meningeal layer of Dura mater, CSF is located between arachnoid and pia mater layers and is reabsorbed via the venous system through arachnoid villi('')
                 -Arachnoid mater: intermediate layer, highly vascular 
                 -Pia mater: inner layer, adhered to brain and spinal cord, contains blood vessels 
           Dural Reflections
              -Dural infoldings: formed by the meningeal layer('meningeal layer.png') of the dura mater reflecting away from the periosteal layer, dragging the other layers of the meninges with it to form six meningeal layers Γ(1.1 Dura mater, .1.2 Arachnoid mater., 1.3 Pia mater., 1.4 Subarachnoidal lymphatic-like membrane., 1.5 Leptomeninges., 1.6 Subarachnoid space.) in the dural reflection
                 -Tentorial notch(''): allows for the brainstem to pass through the dural reflection connecting the cerebral hemispheres to the spinal cord
                 -Tentorium cerebelli: “roof over the posterior fossa”; supports the cerebral hemispheres and lies on top of  the cerebellum; the anterior attachment is the posterior aspect of the sella turcica
                 -3 layers, meningeal layer pulls away from periosteal layer
                 -6 layers for dural reflections, thicker provide more support, foldings inward of meningeal layers to form supporting structure to help support the brain

                    -Horizontal Dural reflection, where brain sits on, and is supported inferiorly: Tentorium Cerebelli “covers posterior fossa” and creates cavity for middle fossa('')

                       -Cerebellum sits beneath the Tentorium Cerebelli
                    -Falx Cerebelli runs from front to back and sits in-between the cerebellum 
           Dural Venous Sinuses('')
              -System for draining blood from the brain; formed in the borders of the dural reflections; returns deoxygenated blood to the heart
                 -Cavernous sinus(''): lies on lateral parts of the Sella Turcica, Provides path for blood from deep cerebral veins('') to internal jugular vein
                 -Sigmoid sinus('Sigmoid sinus'): lateral to foramen magnum, provides path for blood from transverse sinus('') to internal jugular vein
                 -Transverse sinus(''): loops off sigmoid sinus leads to straight sinus(''), provides path for blood from the confluence of sinuses to sigmoid sinus.
                 -Straight sinus: provides path for blood from inferior sagittal sinus('') to the confluence of sinuses
                 -Superior sagittal sinus(''): Provides path for blood from superficial cerebral veins to the confluence of sinuses
                 -Inferior sagittal sinus(''): provides path for blood from inferior cerebral veins to straight sinus
                 -Internal jugular vein: major venous vessel for the skull, brain, superficial face and neck
           Ventricular system('')
                 -Floats and bathes the brain and provides it with nutrients
                 -Closed space within the center of the brain tissue, continuous with the subarachnoid space
                 -Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) that is made in the roof of the ventricles in the choroid plexus('') circulates and is reabsorbed into the venous blood through specializations of the arachnoid (arachnoid villi) into the superior sagittal sinus
                 -Consists of ventricles and related structures (top left to bottom right)
                    -Lateral ventricles (2): C-shaped ventricles that underlie each cerebral hemisphere
                    -Interventricular foramen: provides communication between lateral ventricles and third ventricle
                    -Third ventricle: midline, central ventricle between the right and left thalamus
                    -Cerebral aqueduct: underlies the midbrain; passageway for CSF from third to fourth ventricle
                    -Fourth ventricle: triangular shaped ventricle; overlies the pons and medulla, and under the cerebellum 
                    -Lateral apertures (2): Dual lateral exits for CSF from the fourth ventricle to the subarachnoid space
                    -Median aperture: single midline exit for CSF to circulate around the spinal cord
